RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL 
 
You are hereby summoned to attend a meeting of Ramsey Town Council to be held at 7pm 
on Thursday 22nd October 2026, in The Lavender Room, Ramsey Town Council, Great 
Whyte, Ramsey, when the following items of business will be transacted: - 
 
Please ensure all mobile phones are switched off or turned to silent during the 
meeting. 
The meeting room will open to the public at 18.50. 
 
Lisa Renfree                                      16th October 2026 
   
  
 
  
Town Clerk/RFO 
 
A G E N D A  
 
 
APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE 
 
1. DECLARATIONS OF INTEREST 
To receive declarations from Members as to disclosable pecuniary and other 
interests and the nature of those interests in relation to any agenda item. 
   
2. PUBLIC PARTICIPATION 
    To allow 20 minutes for any members of the public to address the Council.  
 
3. MINUTES 
To approve as a correct record, the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 
8
th
 October 2026 - attached. 
  
4. COUNCILLOR RESIGNATIONS 
Notice is hereby given pursuant to section 87(2) of the Local Government Act 1972 
that due to the resignation of Councillor Ash Austin and Councillor Phil Rose there 
are two vacancies in the Town Council. 
If, within 14 statutory days after the date of this notice, a request for an election to 
fill the vacancy is made in writing to the Returning Officer, Huntingdonshire District 
Council,  Pathfinder  House,  Huntingdon  PE29  3TN  by  ten  electors  of  the town  an 
election will be held.  If no such notice is given the Town Council will fill the vacancy 
by co-option. 
 
5. PLANNING- Members are asked to visit the Huntingdonshire District Council 
Planning Portal to view the plans and documents prior to the meeting. 
 
1.1 26/01809/FUL Erection of a new 2 bed bungalow, 284 Herne Road, Ramsey St 
Mary’s Huntingdon PE26 2TB 
1.2  26/01440/FUL Change of use to a SEN day school (Class F1), erection of a rear 
single storey extension, external alterations to existing two-storey rear extension, 
and associated works including additional car parking, new landscaping, and 
recreation areas, Westward House, Bury Road, Ramsey, Huntingdon PE26 1NA 
1.3 26/01526/FUL Temporary permission for a period of 15 years for the erection of 3 
units for use as retail or community space and associated public realm and 

highway improvements – Pedestrian Island, Great Whyte, Ramsey. This item is on 
the agenda to complete the vote on the substantial motion on 1.1 from the meeting 
of 8
th
 October. The substantive motion is ‘There is insufficient information for 
Ramsey Town Council to be able to support the application.’ If this vote is 
defeated it will return to the original motion ‘To accept the application’ 
 
 Planning – other business 
a) Feedback on Planning online training 21
st
 October. 
b) Feedback on the Development Management Committee reference the David 
Wilson Homes. Cllr S Corney 
c) To agree the representations to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District 
Council in response to their Local Plan consultation (previously circulated) 
 
 
6. MEETING DATES 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council will take place on 12th November 2026 at 
7pm.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
MINUTES OF RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL MEETING 
held at 7pm on Thursday 08 October 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:    Councillors: A Austin, I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, Cllrs S Corney, V 
Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, L Knight, P Rose, R Terrill, J Thompson, L Webster and E Welsh. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk  
 
320. Apologies for Absence. 
 Cllrs A Costello, C Maskell. 
 
321.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made at that point. 
 
322. Public Participation. 
There  was  six  members  of  the  public  who  discussed  planning  1.3,  discussing  the  potential 
199  David  Wilson  Homes  which  was  going  to  be  debated  on  19
th
 October  at  Development 
Management Panel and a question was raised to be answered post that meeting on where 
the community would stand to make a legal challenge. 
 
323. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr L Knight, Councillors voted 13 FOR and 2 
ABSTENSIONS for the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 24
th
 September 2026 
as a correct record. 
 
324.County and District Councillor Update. 
County and District Councillor Cllr H Tobias attended the meeting to feedback on both County 
and District matters. Cllr Tobias outlined two visits to Ashbeach School and Abbey College 
and  commented  on  the  challenges  that  Ashbeach  faced  with  lack  of  SEN  funding  and 
commented on the brilliant discipline of the students in behaviour at Abbey College. As the 
County Councillor Cllr Tobias had been out with the Highways Officer to discuss the state of 
the roads in the community, and the biggest block is the funding to repair underneath the roads 
instead they are only able to fund patching them. Cllr Tobias then went on to discuss the 199 
David Wilson Homes and informed members that further housing would be coming at the RAF 
Upwood   site   and   still   with   no   infrastructure   in   place.   Cllr   Tobias   touched   on   the 
Pedestrianisation and welcomed better communication on the project. Cllr Tobias was asked 
by the Mayor if he had any information on the pilot project on resurfacing the Fen Roads – Cllr 
Tobias  had  not.  Cllr  J  Clarke  asked  Cllr  Tobais  about  the  waste  of  resource  on  the  use  of 
traffic  lights  when  no  work  is  taking  place.  Cllr  Tobias  noted  the  comments.  Cllr  Tobias did 
state you can read what he had been achieving in his two columns in the local newspaper. 
 
Presentation from Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust 
Cllr I Axelsen and Cllr J Aubin declared a non-pecuniary interest on this item as Trustees of 
Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust. 
 
Sam and Sarah from Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust gave a presentation to members with an 
overview of the community group, what they do and what services they provide. Sarah talked 
through the young people’s projects which Ramsey Town Council funding had been covering. 
Cllr Axelsen who is also the Chair of Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust had previously circulated 
the funding figures to members. The funding for the following year would be discussed at the 
following Finance Working Party and form part of the 20278/28 budget. 

 
 
325. Planning Applications for Consideration: 
 
1.1 26/01526/FUL Temporary permission for a period of 15 years for the erection of 3 units 
for use as retail or community space and associated public realm and highway 
improvements – Pedestrian Island, Great Whyte, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr S Corney 
and seconded by Cllr E Welsh Cllr S Corney proposed acceptance of the application. 
Proposed by Cllr A  Austin and seconded by Cllr M Clarke an amendment to Cllr s 
Corney’s proposal ‘There is insufficient information for Ramsey Town Council to be able 
to support the application.’ A vote was taken on the amendment 5 FOR, 3 AGAINST and 
6 ABSTENSIONS. This meant that the amendment became the substantive motion. 
There was confusion for the councillors who voted to abstain as they thought they would 
then be able to vote on the original proposal by Cllr S Corney, this was not the case once 
the amendment had become the substantive motion. The meeting then moved on to 
planning application 1.2  
1.2 25/01301/FUL Erection of owner/site managers dwelling to serve existing caravan site.  
The retention of 14 existing touring caravan pitches, toilet and shower block and 3 holiday 
lodges along with the erection of two new timber holiday lodges and four new holiday 
pods – Riverside Lake and Leisure, Mereside Drove, Ramsey Mereside. Proposed by Cllr 
S Corney and seconded by Cllr P Rose Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for 
the District Council to APPROVE the application. Members were clear their previous 
comments still stood. 
1.3 26/01763/FUL Erection of 3 detached dwellings, 3 detached double garages and 
associated works – Oak Cottage, Forty Foot Bank, Ramsey Forty Foot. Cllrs A Austin, P 
Rose and S Corney declared a non-pecuniary interest as they knew the applicant. 
Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr J Bufton for District Council to 
APPROVE the application - Ramsey Town Council voted 6 FOR, 8 AGAINST and 1 
ABSTENTION The majority vote was for the application to be REFUSED. Members 
shared the concerns of the neighbouring residents in attendance. 
1.4 26/01763/FUL/26/01764/LBC Proposed conversion and extension of existing curtilage 
listed outbuilding into a separate, independently owned dwellinghouse – Bodsey House, 
Bodsey Toll Road, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr P Rose 
Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to APPROVE the 
application 
1.5 25/01433/FUL /26/00045/REFUSL Land Far West of Romany Cottage, Bucks Drove, 
Ramsey St Marys. Proposed self-build dwelling to be used as site manager’s house.  
Appeal against refusal. Cllr J Clarke declared a non-pecuniary as a neighbour to the 
applicant. Proposed by Cllr M Clarke and seconded Ramsey Town Council 13 FOR and 2 
ABSTENTIONS for the District Council to keep the REFUSAL in place. Their previous 
comments stood. 
 
326. Planning – other business 
a) Latest Planning Tracker – noted 
b) Planning online training- Members were reminded of the online planning training that 
would take place on zoom on 21
st
 October 2026. The Clerk was asked to circulate the 
invitation again. 
 
327. Finance Items 
a) Financial summary – Cash book to 30/09/2026 – noted 

b) Expenditure Transactions to be approved. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by 
Cllr S Fice Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the expenditure transactions 
to be APPROVED. 
c) Grant applications – The Clerk informed members that 13 applications had been 
received and they would go to the next Finance Working Party and approved at the 
November Full Council meeting. 
d) Budget 2027/28 – Cllr S Fice informed members that the budget packs would be sent 
out in the following week. 
 
328.Working Party Updates 
 Members to receive an update from the Chairs of each Working Party – the Clerk 
apologised it had not gone out with the agenda papers but circulated that day. 
 
329. Working Party Recommendations 
 Economic Development – Members were informed that the SLA agreement for the 
Discover Huntingdonshire website. 
 Communications – Members were informed that the Newtown Road Play Park 
Consultation had been completed and the response was overwhelmingly positive. 
 
330.Town Mayor’s and Clerk’s Correspondence 
a) Civic Service Feedback – Cllr V Fendley fed back to members on how much people 
appreciated the Civic Service and its community spirit and that a lovely handwritten letter had 
been received by the High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire which would be in the office if any 
member wished to read it. 
b) Zebra Crossing Location, Abbey College Local Highways Initiative Bid – Members were 
informed by Cllr V Fendley that the wording on the consultation had been changed as 
Ramsey Town Council had not supported the zebra crossing due to the loss of parking 
spaces it would cause outside St Thomas a Becket Church. The Clerk was asked to forward 
the link to members. 
c) Local Highways Initiative Bid (Ramsey St Mary’s Buffer zones) update. The Clerk tabled 
the information received from Highways that the bid had not been successful. Further 
clarification had been asked for and it would go to the Amenities, Highways and Leisure 
Working Party. 
d) FOI Feedback – The Clerk informed members that the FOI had been responded to and no 
further communication had taken place. 
e) Newsletter Distribution – The Clerk informed members that the newsletter was being 
distributed and being well received. 
f) Development Management Committee – The Mayor informed members that the DMC 
meeting would take place on the 19
th
 October and members could attend in person, register 
to speak, or watch via zoom. Cllr S Corney would be representing the views at the meeting of 
Ramsey Town Council. 
g) Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan – The Mayor informed members that the 
referendum for the NHP would take place on Thursday 26
th
 November 2026. 
 
331. Car Park Land Lease 
To discuss the Heads of Terms for the lease – the Clerk had previously circulated the Heads 
of Terms for comment. Cllr J Clarke asked if the Clerk could push for a longer lease than 50 
years. No other comments were asked to be sent back to HDC. Once the lease has gone 
through HDC Legal it will come to members for sign off. 
 
332. Attendances at Meetings and Organisations 
a) Flood Action Planning Meeting – Cllr J Thompson fed back to members about the meeting 
and that the flood action group should be community led, focussed, and tested. 

b) Emergency Planning for the Future – Cllr V Fendley informed members that the meeting 
had 16 residents in attendance a very robust discussion had taken place. Cllr J Thompson 
had taken on the responsibility of outing the actions into the provided template. 
c) LVEP Conference – Cllr V Fendley explained the LVEP positioning starting at the bottom 
with Discover Ramsey, then Discover Huntingdonshire, Loval Visitor Economy Partnership 
and topped by Visit England. Cllr L Knight fed back to members about the Local Visitor 
Economy Forum Conference. It was a very positive meeting with a shout out to Ramsey for 
signing the Service Level Agreement for Discover Huntingdonshire. Both Cllr L K night and 
Cllr V Fendley both attended and sat on the table with Visit England. 
 
333. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 22nd October 
(Planning) at 7pm. 
 
 
Town Mayor_______________________________________Date___________________

events.content: Ramsey Town Council meeting including public participation, discussion on councillor vacancies, planning applications (including 284 Herne Road, Westward House on Bury Road, and the Pedestrian Island on Great Whyte), and Local Plan consultation responses. The public room opens at 18:50.

governance.title: Town Council Vacancies Due to Councillor Resignations
governance.summary: Notice given of two council vacancies following the resignations of Councillor Ash Austin and Councillor Phil Rose. An election will be held if requested in writing by ten electors within 14 statutory days to the Returning Officer at Huntingdonshire District Council; otherwise, the Town Council will fill the vacancies by co-option.

governance.title: Planning Applications and Consultations Review
governance.summary: Council members to review planning applications including a 2-bed bungalow at 284 Herne Road (Ramsey St Mary's), change of use to a SEN day school at Westward House (Bury Road), and complete a vote on the retail/community space units proposed for the Pedestrian Island on Great Whyte. Also discussing online planning training feedback, David Wilson Homes development feedback, and representations for the HDC Local Plan consultation.

Foreword 
 
On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, welcome to the Neighbourhood Plan for our Parish area which 
covers  the  settlements  of Ramsey;  Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & 
Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small part of Pondersbridge.  
 
The Neighbourhood Plan sets out the vision, objectives and policies to ensure that 
the town and the villages maintain their character, appearance and uniqueness over 
the period up to 2046; whilst helping to facilitate growth. The town is undergoing 
significant planned development, and the Neighbourhood Plan aims to ensure that 
the  planned  growth  respects  the  important  features  that  make our  communities 
distinctive.  
 
The Neighbourhood Plan seeks to protect and enhance the natural and built environment of the 
parish which forms the character of where we live. 
 
The Neighbourhood Plan has been drawn up by a Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group on behalf of 
Ramsey Town Council which is the designated body for the plan area and provided the funding and 
support  to  enable  the  plan  to  go  ahead. The 
Neighbourhood Plan  has  gone through  a  number  of 
stages including statutory public consultation and an 
Independent  Examination. The  Neighbourhood  Plan 
was  found  to  be  appropriate  by  the  Independent 
Examiner who published their report in late August 
2026. 
 
The   process now involves a   local   referendum 
requiring a majority ‘Yes’ vote of all those voting in 
the referendum for it to be accepted. In the event 
of a ‘Yes’ vote, Huntingdonshire District Council will 
proceed to ‘make’ the Neighbourhood Plan for the 
Parish of Ramsey. 
 
The  Neighbourhood  Plan  sets  down  a  series  of 
planning    policies    which    will    form    part    of 
Huntingdonshire’s  wider  statutory  development 
plan.  The  Neighbourhood  Plan will  be  used  for 
determining   planning   applications   alongside the 
Huntingdonshire Local Plan. 
 
It  is  intended  that  the  policies  will  be  reviewed 
periodically to monitor the cumulative effects of the 
policies  and,  if  necessary,  make  changes  to  keep 
them up to date and relevant.  
 
So, our personal thanks to all those who have driven the process so far and thank you for taking 
the time to consider the Neighbourhood Plan. 
        
Councillor Mrs Val Fendley      
Mayor of Ramsey Town Council 
 
Sarah Mullineux 
Lead of the Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group

Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version) 
 
9 
Introduction 
 
1. Background 
 
1.1 The Localism Act 2011 introduced a new type of Community Led Plan.  Communities now 
have the right to produce a Neighbourhood Plan, setting out policies on the development 
and use of land.  Developing a Neighbourhood Plan is a way for communities to play a greater 
role in determining the future of their area. A plan period of 2046 has been chosen to match 
the plan period of the emerging Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2046. 
 
1.2 The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan forms part of the statutory Development Plan.  
This means that Huntingdonshire District Council will determine planning applications within 
the Parish in accordance with the development plan which includes this Neighbourhood Plan 
unless material planning considerations indicate otherwise 
(see section 38(6)
1
 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase 
Act 2004). 
 
1.3 This Neighbourhood Plan is a Community Led Plan.  It has 
been  prepared  by a  Steering  Group  made  up  of local 
residents and councillors on behalf of the Town Council with 
professional   support.   It   has   been   informed   by   public 
participation and consultation firstly carried out informally 
in    2025 with    the    local    community. The    formal 
Neighbourhood  Plan  preparation  process will involve  two 
statutory  periods  of  public  consultation;  this  is  the  first 
statutory consultation to undertaken in 2026 as prescribed 
in Regulations
2
. 
 
1.4 A Neighbourhood Plan is a planning document and is about 
the use and development of land. Neighbourhood planning 
gives communities more control over the future of their area 
by giving local people the chance to have their say on what 
happens where they live. 
 
1.5 A neighbourhood   plan   can   establish   general   planning 
policies for  the development and use of land in a particular area. Plans can include local 
priorities, planning policies, proposals for improving an area or providing new facilities or 
infrastructure and allocation of key sites for development. 
 
1.6 Neighbourhood planning  is  a  tool  to  promote  sustainable  growth  and  will  not  be  able  to 
prevent  development  in  an  area.  Neighbourhood  plans  can  only  include  proposals  for  an 
equal  (or  greater)  amount  of  growth  than  is  set  out  in  the  local  authority's  development 
plan. They must also accord with national planning policy 
 
 
2. Sustainability Appraisal (SA) and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) 
 
2.1 Every Neighbourhood  Plan  needs  to  consider  the  need  for  a  Sustainability  Appraisal 
(incorporating a Strategic Environmental Assessment) for the Neighbourhood Plan.  SA is a 
mechanism  for  considering  and  communicating  the  impacts  of  an  emerging  plan,  and 
potential alternatives in terms of key sustainability issues. 
 
 
1
 http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/5/section/38 
2
 https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2012/637/contents/made 

Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version) 
 
10 
2.2 The Town Council considers that there will be no significant environmental effects arising 
from the Neighbourhood Plan. They have produced a SEA and HRA Screening Assessment for 
the Neighbourhood Plan which has demonstrated that a SEA is not required. Consequently, 
no SA incorporating an SEA has been undertaken for the Neighbourhood Plan. 
 
 
3. National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 
 
3.1 Throughout this  Neighbourhood  Plan  reference  is  made  to  the  National  Planning  Policy 
Framework (NPPF).  The NPPF sets out the government’s planning policies for England and 
how these are expected to be applied.  It was first published on 27 March 2012, with the 
NPPF version
3
 against  which  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  was produced  and  examined being 
published in December 2024. It is also supplemented by Planning Practice Guidance. 
 
3.2 The NPPF provides a framework to produce locally distinctive Neighbourhood Plans which 
reflect the needs and aspirations of the community.   
 
3.3 The Government had consulted on a new draft NPPF
4
 over the period from December 2025 
to March 2026. The draft NPPF proposed for the first time there is a clear set of separate 
policies  for  both  plan-making  and  decision-making.  This  is  intended  to  achieve  three 
principal objectives, namely to: 
 
• Ensure national planning policy is accessible and understandable for  everyone who 
uses it; 
• Establish  a  comprehensive  suite  of  national  policies  on  general  planning  matters 
which  will  apply  across  the  country,  to  avoid  these  matters  being  repeated  or 
deviated from in locally-produced plans; and 
• Make  the  policy  which  it  contains  more  ‘rules-based’  and  certain,  and  so  more 
capable of supporting timely and consistent. 
 
3.4 The Neighbourhood Plan preparation did take account of the new draft NPPF as it gave a 
clear direction of travel. The Government then published the new NPPF
5
 in mid-August 2026 
shortly before  the  Independent  Examination  of  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  ended. The 
Government has incorporated policies  relating  to  traveller  sites, previously set  out  in 
Planning Policy for Traveller Sites, within the relevant chapters of the NPPF.  
 
3.5 The Neighbourhood Plan contributes towards the achievement of sustainable development. 
More detail on the ways in which this Plan addresses sustainable development is included 
within the Basic Conditions Statement that accompanies the Plan. 
 
 
4. Planning Practice Guidance 
 
4.1 Planning Practice  Guidance
6
 sets  out  the  government’s  advice  on  how  to  undertake 
neighbourhood planning within England. This is set out in detail within Section 41 of Planning 
Practice Guidance. Planning Practice Guidance also sets out national advice on a wide range 
of planning topics.

5. Structure of Neighbourhood Plan 
 
5.1 The Neighbourhood   Plan   includes   three themed   sections: Community;   Heritage   & 
Environment; and Infrastructure. 
 
 
 
5.2 These are issues that are important to the community and within each section policies are 
included to guide the development and use of land. Each Policy contains an introduction and 
explanatory  text  followed  by  the  Policy  itself  in  coloured  text. Following the  themed 
sections, the Neighbourhood Plan contains an implementation and delivery section. 
 
 
The Development Plan 
 
6. Background 
 
6.1 The ‘Development Plan’ for Ramsey Parish (Ramsey;  Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; 
Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small 
part of Pondersbridge) is made up of 3 main components as follows:

6.2 All policies  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  should  be  read  in  conjunction  with  the 
Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036. When determining proposals for development, no policy 
will be applied in isolation and account will be taken of all relevant policies. Even if the 
proposed Local Government Reorganisation occurs,  the Development Plan will not change 
until any replacement Development Plan is adopted. 
 
 
7. Relationship to Huntingdonshire Local Plan 
 
7.1 The  Huntingdonshire Local Plan  to  2036
7
 was adopted  in May 2019. Any  reference  in  this 
Neighbourhood  Plan  to  ‘Local  Plan’  or  ‘Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan’  means  the 
Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036.  
 
7.2 The purpose of the Local Plan is to set out: 
• the strategy for development in the whole of Huntingdonshire; 
• policies for managing development; and 
• details of sites for development to meet the needs of Huntingdonshire. 
 
7.3 The District Council is in the process of undertaking a Local Plan Update
8
 to be known as the 
Huntingdonshire Local  Plan  to  2046.  The Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  to  2046 was 
published for consultation during November and December 2025. There is no obligation for 
a Neighbourhood Plan to be in general conformity with an emerging Local Plan; although it 
is sensible to look to ensure that inconsistency is avoided. Although, there is no certainty 
that  allocations  or  proposals  identified  in  the  Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  will  be 
carried forward into the later stages.  
 
7.4 In broad terms the Preferred Options Draft Local Plan to 2046
9
 looked to continue the same 
approach  to  the  settlement hierarchy.  Limited  additional  allocations for  housing  and 
employment are proposed at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the 
north-eastern  and south-eastern sides  of  Ramsey  town. A  that  time  there were  two  main 
areas of consistency that need to be considered in the context of future general conformity 
between the emerging Neighbourhood Plan and the emerging Local Plan Review. These were 
in relation to a protected settlement break between Ramsey and Upwood Airfield/Bury, and 
the area between Ramsey Rural Museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp which the Neighbourhood 
Plan proposes as Local Green Space.  
 
7.5 Any  reference  in  this  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  ‘Local  Plan Update’  means  the emerging 
Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2046. Huntingdonshire  District  Council  are scheduled  to 
publish the  Proposed  Submission  Local  Plan Update  to  2046 for  consultation  across 
September and October 2026. That will then need to be submitted to the Secretary of State 
which is anticipated to be in December 2026. Followed by the examination process during 
2027, with adoption anticipated in 2028.  
 
7.6 The Proposed Submission Local Plan Update to 2046 still proposes allocations for housing and 
employment at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the south-eastern 
side  of  Ramsey  town. Together  with  a  housing  allocation  at  Ramsey  Forty  Foot on  the 
southern side.  
 
7.7 Even if the proposed Local Government Reorganisation occurs, the Local Plan Update would 
still be likely to be completed by the new Council if appropriate.

8. Strategic policies for the purposes of neighbourhood planning 
 
8.1 The system  of  neighbourhood  planning  allows Parish and  Town  Councils  to  produce 
neighbourhood plans to guide development at a local level. One of the requirements of such 
plans was that they should be in line with the 'strategic policies' of the adopted development 
plan for  the local area. Although, this legal requirement was removed in late March 2026 
during  the  preparation  of  this Neighbourhood  Plan. As  preparation  started  with  this 
requirement in place, reference is still made to it. 
 
8.2 Huntingdonshire District Council as the Local Planning Authority defines which policies are 
to  be  considered  'strategic'  with  regard  to  the production  of  a  neighbourhood plan. They 
consider that some of the policies and all the allocations within the Huntingdonshire Local 
Plan to  2036 are to be considered  'strategic'  for  the  purposes  of  neighbourhood  planning. 
Details  of  which  policies  are  deemed  ‘strategic’  is  set  out  in  the  introduction  of  the 
Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036
10
. 
 
 
9. Surrounding Neighbourhood Plans 
 
9.1 The Neighbourhood Plan was developed 
with consideration of whether there are 
any  other  Neighbourhood  Plans  being 
developed which share a boundary with 
Ramsey Parish. To the south of Ramsey 
is the village of Bury. Ramsey, Bury and 
the former Upwood Airfield collectively 
form the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area 
in the Local Plan.  
 
9.2 The Bury Neighbourhood   Plan   was 
‘made’ on 19 May 2021. The Bury 
Neighbourhood Plan is now part of the 
adopted  Development  Plan. The Bury 
Neighbourhood Plan identifies a number 
of   issues   that   have   cross   boundary 
implications   including   a settlement 
boundary  and  a  protected  settlement 
break.   Strategic   extensions   to   the 
village of Bury at Upwood Airfield also 
have cross  boundary  implications  for 
the Parish of Ramsey.  
 
9.2 Bury  Parish  Council  are  in  the  early 
stages of undertaking the First Review of the Bury Neighbourhood Plan, having undertaken 
consultation on a draft of the First Review from July to September 2026. 
 
9.3 The other  neighbouring  Parishes in  Huntingdonshire are Farcet,  Holme,  Wood  Walton, 
Upwood   and   the   Raveleys and   Warboys.   None of   these   Parishes   are   working   on 
Neighbourhood Plans. 
 
9.4 The Parish  of Ramsey lies  on  the  northern  edge  of  Huntingdonshire  and abuts  the 
neighbouring District of Fenland to the north. Whittlesey to the north has a Neighbourhood 
Plan that was ‘made’ on 22 May 2023. Doddington lies to the north-east, it is working on a 
Neighbourhood  Plan  having  produced a Draft  Plan  in  2025. Whittlesey  Parish  covers  the 
majority  of  the  village  of  Pondersbridge,  but  there  are  no  particular  cross  boundary

implications  that  need  considering. The  other  neighbouring  Parish in  Fenland  is Benwick, 
they are not working on a Neighbourhood Plan. 
 
 
10. Designation of Ramsey Parish as a Neighbourhood Planning Area 
 
10.1 A  formal application
11
 was  made  by Ramsey  Town Council  in January 2024 as a ‘relevant 
body’ under Section 61G of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) for the 
designation of a neighbourhood area in order to develop a neighbourhood plan. The area of 
the Neighbourhood Plan is based upon the parish boundary, which was seen as appropriate 
as this area is recognised as the distinct communities of Ramsey; Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey 
Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & 
a  small  part  of  Pondersbridge. The  request  was  that  the  Parish  be  recognised  as  a 
Neighbourhood Area for the purpose of producing a neighbourhood plan, in accordance with 
the Neighbourhood Planning Regulations 2012. 
 
10.2 Huntingdonshire District Council designated
12
 the Parish of Ramsey as a neighbourhood area 
on 6 February 2024. 
 
 
11. Consultation with the Local Community 
 
11.1 Since the designation of Ramsey as a neighbourhood area, various elements of consultation 
have been undertaken regarding the future planning of the Parish. Details of the consultation 
undertaken to date are set out in the Consultation Statement that accompanies this Plan. 
Early informal public participation and consultation was undertaken in 2025. The preparation 
process for  a Neighbourhood  Plan is prescribed  in Regulations
13
 and  this involves  two 
statutory periods of public consultation.  
 
11.2 Consultation on the draft plan was undertaken in early 2026. The comments received from 
local residents and consultees were considered and influenced this Submission version of the 
Neighbourhood Plan. The process then involved further consultation on this Submission Plan 
undertaken  by Huntingdonshire  District  Council in  May  and  June  2026.  The  Independent 
Examiner then considered the representations made on the Submission Plan during July and 
August 2026 before producing their Independent Examiner’s Report in late August 2026. 
 
 
Other Planning Documents 
 
12.1 In addition to the Development Plan there are also a number of other planning documents 
known as Supplementary Planning Documents
14
 which cover the whole of Huntingdonshire. 
These include: 
• Huntingdonshire Design Guide SPD (2017) 
• Cambridgeshire Flood and Water SPD (2017)  
• Wind Energy Development in Huntingdonshire SPD (2014)  
• Developer  Contributions  SPD  (2011) (with  updated  costs annually  or  successor 
documents)  
• Huntingdonshire Landscape and Townscape SPD (2022)

12.3 Part of the town of Ramsey is within the Ramsey 
Conservation  Area. Somewhat  confusingly,  the 
Ramsey Conservation  Area  extends across  part 
of the neighbouring village and Parish of Bury. 
There    is a Conservation    Area Character 
Assessment
18
 for   this   Conservation   Area. A 
character   appraisal where   published has   a 
purpose  to  identify  and  record  those  special 
qualities  that  make  up  the  architectural  and 
historic character.  
 
 
The Communities of Ramsey 
 
13.1 The Parish covers an area of 6,361 hectares. The Parish of Ramsey comprises the distinct 
communities of Ramsey; Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St 
Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small part of Pondersbridge.  
 
13.2 The town is the largest settlement and 
is  about 14 miles  (22 km)  north  of 
Huntingdon. The town of Ramsey grew 
up    around    Ramsey    Abbey,    an 
important  Benedictine  monastery.  In 
the order of precedence for abbots in 
Parliament,  Ramsey  was  third  after 
Glastonbury  and  St  Albans.  The  town 
manor is built on the site of (and using 
materials from) the ancient Abbey and 
is  the  seat  of  the  Lords  de  Ramsey, 
major  landowners  in  Lincolnshire  and 
Cambridgeshire.  The  remains  of  the 
Abbey  are  now  home  to  part  of  the 
town's secondary school.  
 
13.3 The     Ramsey Conservation     Area 
Character Assessment
19

Vision 
 
16.1 The following vision has been developed for the Neighbourhood Plan: 
 
To  provide  a  planning  framework  and  policies  that  will 
result  in  sustainable  growth  for  the  local  community, 
ensuring  that  appropriate  infrastructure,  services  and 
facilities are provided whilst also conserving the distinct 
character of the town and villages that form the overall 
community of Ramsey. 
 
 
Objectives 
 
16.2 The following objectives have been set out for the Neighbourhood Plan: 
 
(A) Promote sustainable development and infrastructure  
 
• Collaborate through the production of development plans and the determination of 
planning applications  including  pre-application  engagement with  Huntingdonshire 
District  Council and  developers  of  individual  parcels to ensure  that growth  of  the 
Ramsey Spatial Planning Area delivers sustainable growth without resulting in further 
coalescence with Bury and Upwood Airfield. 
• Ensure that new development is of high-quality design, is built to a high sustainability 
standard and includes or contributes to open space and community facilities. 
• Ensure that the design and location of new development is resilient to the effects of 
climate change and flooding. 
• Ensure that new development integrates into the existing town or village including 
linking  all  developments  to  the  rest  of  the town  or village  with  footpaths,  where 
appropriate. 
• Locate new development such that current problems with congestion, parking and 
road safety are not exacerbated and, if possible, reduced. 
 
(B) Conserve and enhance the built and natural environment 
 
• Protect, enhance and conserve the open spaces; landscape; views; and biodiversity 
across the town and villages. 
• Use land efficiently and to preserve high quality agricultural land. 
• Conserve  and  enhance  the built environment  of  the town  and villages, including 
through  ensuring that  new  development  respects  or  enhances  the distinctive 
character and appearance of the area in which it is sited. 
 
(C) Protect and develop the communities of Ramsey 
 
• Protect  and  preserve  important community assets  including  its  local  services  and 
facilities by encouraging the retention and growth of community facilities. 
• Continue to improve the facilities on offer to support the local community, including 
through outreach services. 
• Continue to support community events.

Community Aspirations 
 
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For 
the Theme – Community, the following are the community aspirations: 
 
Community 
 
The Town  Council  and  Neighbourhood Plan  want  to  support the  various  communities  that 
collectively  make  up  the  parish  of  Ramsey. A  vibrant  and flourishing community includes 
supporting families; encouraging the provision of places to live, work, stay and play; with suitable 
provision of housing including a local connection for housing and affordable housing.  
 
The communities of Ramsey need suitable resilience to adapt to changing circumstances and be 
supported  to  allow  suitable  access  to  services  and  facilities  despite  the  relative  geographic 
isolation.  
 
Resilience also needs to cater for ageing population needs; this includes the provision of specialist 
supported accommodation such as extra care housing or supported living schemes for people of 
all ages with care and support needs. Provision of adult mental health supported accommodation 
and  provision  for  adults  with  learning  disabilities  needs  to  be  provided  as  part  of  an  overall 
balanced and mixed community. 
 
It is an aspiration to ensure that community clubs for  all ages are available and that access to 
adult education is available locally. 
 
Adequate provision of services in proportion to the growth is imperative.  Additional services or 
replacement or extension of existing community buildings such as the library, community centre 
needs  to  be  factored  in. The  communities  want  a  holistic  and  joined  up  approach  so  that 
development,  infrastructure  and services  are  set  up  in  a  harmonious,  cohesive  and  sustainable 
way. 
 
Education 
 
Education needs to be fit for purpose and be well located; including being accessible safely for all 
ages by active travel methods including by foot and bicycle.  
 
Suitable  and  adequate  early  years  provision to  meet  the  differing  needs  of  families.  Such  as 
through day nurseries, full day care, sessional provisional, childminders and wraparound care to 
provide breakfast and after school provision term-time between the hours of 8am and 6pm; need 
to be available in order to allow parents the opportunity to return to work. Additional capacity is 
required across  schools to meet demand. In terms of wider education, access to adult education 
should be available locally.

19. Definition of ‘Built-up Area’ (Settlement Boundary) 
 
19.1 Ramsey town has planned strategic  growth on sites allocated in the Local Plan. However, 
there has been pressure  for planning  applications to come forward  for  residential 
development on greenfield sites which are not allocated. Such speculative development in 
addition to the allocated sites has the potential to undermine the strategic policies of the 
Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 in terms of the distribution of housing across the district. 
It also has the potential to affect the distinctive character and separate identity of Ramsey 
and the adjacent village of Bury as separate and distinct settlements.  
 
19.2 Ramsey  town is part of the ‘Ramsey Spatial Planning Area’ in Policy LP 2 - Strategy  for 
Development.  Policy  LP  7 - Spatial  Planning  Areas,  supports  development  where  it  is 
appropriately  located  within  a  built-up  area  of  an  identified  Spatial  Planning  Area 
settlement. The Local Plan does not specify any specific housing requirement for the villages 
of Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; nor for  the 

Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version) 
 
31 
part of Pondersbridge which are all deemed as ‘small settlements’ in the Local Plan. There 
is an overall allowance for windfall development to come forward across the collective 73 
small settlements in the Local Plan. 
 
19.3 The Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 does not identify a settlement boundary for these 
villages; instead, it  moves  to  use  of a definition of ‘built-up area’. Policy  LP 9 – Small 
Settlements, supports development where it is appropriately located within a built-up area 
of a small settlement. This is what is known as windfall development as it relates to housing 
coming forward on sites not specifically allocated for housing. 
 
19.4 A settlement boundary is proposed for the town of Ramsey. As this will be contiguous with 
the  built-up  area  of  the  adjoining  village  of  Bury in  some  places;  as  explained in the 
Settlement  Boundary  Methodology document we have  ensured that  consistency  with  the 
settlement  boundary  in  the  Bury Neighbourhood Plan has  taken 
place. 
 
19.5 For Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & 
Ramsey  St  Mary’s a settlement  boundary  is proposed  to  be 
identified to  define  the  ‘built-up  area’ as  referred  to  in  the 
Huntingdonshire   Local   Plan   to   2036. The   small   part   of 
Pondersbridge  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  on  its  own  falls 
below  the  size  parameter  of  30  homes  in  the  Local  Plan  to  be 
identified  as  a  built-up  area. Therefore,  as  explained  in  the 
Settlement   Boundary   Methodology document,   no   settlement 
boundary   for   Pondersbridge   has been established   in   the 
Neighbourhood Plan. 
 
19.6 The settlement boundary  of these  settlements serves a  specific 
purpose  in  that  it  is  intended  to direct the  growth  of  the 
settlement and  enable development  to  take  place  in  a  coherent 
manner,  maintaining  the  structure  and  form  of  the  existing  settlement  geography as  the 
Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036 envisages.  In  addition,  the  boundary  will  protect  the 
landscape setting of the villages.  
 
19.7 The Huntingdonshire Townscape SPD for Ramsey identifies wording that says, ‘Reflect the 
existing built forms and local relationship with the street in any new development’. Policy 1 
of the NP refers to taking into account the existing built form, layout and structure of the 
surrounding area. 
 
19.8 This is intended to cover the wide array of factors that contribute to the distinctiveness of 
how a place looks, works and functions. In terms of structure, we mean factors such as the 
configuration,  the    arrangement  of  the  built  elements  in  a  particular  form,  figure,  or 
combination. 
 
19.9 The National Design Guide suggests that structure can be a separate consideration to built 
form or layout.  For  example,  M2 of National Design Guide looks for  a clear structure and 
hierarchy of streets. It goes on to identify in relation to Layout that: 
“A layout shows how routes and blocks of development are arranged and relate to one 
another to create streets, open spaces and buildings. It defines: 
the structure or settlement pattern; 
the grain, or the pattern of development blocks and plots; and 
the broad distribution of different uses, and their densities or building heights.” 
 
19.10 The National Design Guide also refers to the structure of blocks and routes that this creates; 
as well as open space, its location and structure need careful consideration.

20. Protected Settlement Break 
 
20.1 Parts of Bury immediately abut the town of Ramsey, together with Upwood Airfield the two 
settlements form the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area. The Upwood Airfield area actually falls 
mostly in the Parish of Bury, with the northern part partly in the Parish of Ramsey and the 
western side in the Parish of Upwood. The inter-relationship between the various Parishes 
can be seen on the map below.

 Parish Boundaries 
 
 
20.2 The Parish boundary between Bury and Ramsey was established before much of the growth 
and development occurred. Over time a degree of coalescence between Bury and Ramsey 
has already occurred. The northern part of Bury around Signal Road is contiguous with the 
main  part  of  Ramsey,  as  such  although  spatially  part  of  Bury, it  physically  and  visually 
appears  as  an  extension  to  Ramsey.  The  two  settlements  are  however  two  distinct 
communities and are in two separate but contiguous Parishes.  
 
20.2 The inter-relationship between Ramsey and Bury can be considered in relation to the two 
broad areas of: 1. East of the B1040; and 2. West of the B1040. As the B1040 for part of its 
length  forms  the Parish  boundary on  the  north-south  alignment,  this  provides  a  logical 
feature to choose as the central point to work from in order to undertake an assessment. 
 
20.4 East of the B1040 - There are in fact no gaps remaining between the two Parishes of Ramsey 
and Bury to the east of the B1040. However, there is a gap between the northern part of 
Bury around Signal Road and the main part of Bury village. This remaining gap is the only 
visual and physical separation between the main cores of Bury and Ramsey. Consequently, 
the Bury Neighbourhood Plan has identified this as a Protected Settlement Break as the only 
gap remaining to prevent the complete coalescence of Ramsey and Bury.

20.5 The importance of the gap between Low Bury and White Arches on Bury Road was confirmed 
in appeal APP/H0520/W/16/3155400 which was dismissed in November 2016. Ramsey and 
Bury  have  already  coalesced  in  part  over  past  decades,  this  means  that  the  remaining 
physical and visual breaks that remain are even more important to protect. Land to the east 
of Bury Road between Low Bury and White Arches along with the land to the rear running 
back  to  the  golf  course  was  deemed  important  to  retain  as  undeveloped  to  prevent 
coalescence. Consequently,  that  area  became  a  protected  settlement  break  in  the  made 
Bury Neighbourhood Plan. There is no need for the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan 
to do anything further in this area to prevent coalescence. 
 
20.6 West of the B1040 - Bury has grown, including through the recent development of Longland 
Crescent  to  the  west  of  Upwood  Road.  Ramsey  has  grown,  including  through  the  recent 
development of Frost Way and Stonemason Way. This recent housing development has led 
to the greater threat of coalescence on the western side between Ramsey, Bury and Upwood 
Airfield. There is a wedge of countryside remaining between the northern side of Upwood 
Airfield,  the  western  side  of  Longland  Crescent  and  the  southern  side  of housing  on  the 
south-western fringe of the town of Ramsey. 
 
20.7 Given  that  the  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  proposes  that  the  ‘Ramsey  Spatial 
Planning Area’ has allocations for 895 homes and 2 hectares of employment land there is a 
real threat that unchecked growth could lead to further coalescence between Ramsey and 
Bury.  The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  does  not  include  any policy  to prevent  the 
coalescence of Ramsey and Bury, although the Bury Neighbourhood Plan does. In terms of 
consistency,  it  is  appropriate  for  the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  also  secure  this 
important community objective of retaining the distinct settlements of Ramsey and Bury. 
 
20.8 There  is  also  the  potential  through  further  urban  extension  for  development  on  Upwood 
Airfield to lead to coalescence on the western side between Ramsey and Bury. Part of the 
northern part of Upwood Airfield lies within Ramsey Parish, although if developed spatially 
this area would effectively operate as part of Upwood Airfield. The allocations at Upwood

20.10 Retaining  a  physical  and  visual  separation  in  this  area  would  be  important  to  retain  the 
distinct  separate  identity  of  Ramsey  and  Bury.  The  principle  of  preventing  further 
coalescence  between  the  two  settlements  has  been  established  in  the  made  Bury 
Neighbourhood  Plan.  As  such  it  has  been  found  to  be  an  appropriate  strategy  by  the 
Independent Examiner who undertook the examination of the Bury Neighbourhood Plan. It is 
important that adjoining Neighbourhood Areas have regard to cross boundary issues in the 
interest of consistency and so as not to undermine other parts of the Development Plan. 
 
20.11 Consequently, it is considered to be necessary and appropriate in the Ramsey Neighbourhood 
Plan to set out a suitable policy approach to prevent further coalescence between Ramsey 
and  Bury.  As  such  a protected settlement  break  between  Ramsey  and  the  planned  urban 
edge of Upwood Airfield is therefore included in the Neighbourhood Plan. This is important 
to protect distinct identities of Ramsey and Bury as separate settlements.

currently  allocated  for  development,  it  is  an

Given   its   inter-relationship   to   the   existing 
development  on  Upwood  Airfield,  without  pre-

reasonable to take the position that development 
continuing  on  the  airfield  is likely  to  occur. The 
Local Plan to 2046 is considering it as an emerging 
allocation now known as allocation ‘Bury 3’. 
 
20.13 The  protected  settlement  break  forms  an  important  green  corridor  which  would  assist  in 
retaining the identity of the two existing settlements. It also provides opportunities for new 
green  infrastructure  and/or  biodiversity  enhancement  to  support  the  delivery  of  the 
strategic allocations. It is considered that the edge of the former Upwood airfield runway 
forms  an  existing  defensible  boundary  that  is  more  appropriate  to  form  the  southern 
boundary  of  the  protected  settlement  break,  rather  than  the  current  allocated  site 
boundaries which are further south. The northern and eastern boundaries of the protected 
settlement  break  is  to  be  the  existing  and  planned  current  edge  of  the  built-up  area  of 
Ramsey and Bury respectively. 
 
20.14 More information on the importance of the Protected Settlement Break is contained in the 
Settlement Boundary Methodology document.

adjacent to the villages.

Community Aspirations 
 
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For

Heritage & Tourism 
 
The parish is home to a wealth of heritage assets, and the historic environment has been identified 
through public consultation as being of particular importance to local residents. Specifically, it is 
a community aspiration to ensure that the heritage is adequately protected and supported. Events 
and assets such as the rural museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp are important both to the heritage 
of the area and the tourism offer. 
 
Potential linkages to proposed major tourism provision at Bedford should be considered to see how 
the wider sub region can benefit from tourism investment and visitors. 
 
In order to protect the heritage of the area, protection of areas like Stocking Fen and the area 
north  of  Tesco should  be  secured. Retaining  Ramsey  and  Bury  as distinct  settlements  is 
fundamental to the history of Ramsey; so, protecting a gap between Bury and Ramsey through 
maintaining a settlement break is a significant community aspiration.  
 
The agricultural origins of the parish are a fundamental part of the character of the area. The 
preservation of agriculture and the agricultural heritage and culture is therefore important.  
 
Great Fen & Biodiversity 
 
The Great Fen project extends into Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s, linkages to the Great 
Fen waterways plan and visitor centre is important.  
 
The  biodiversity of  the  area and the protection  of  green  spaces is  important  to  allow  the 
communities  to enjoy  the  outside  for  recreation  and  views;  whilst  limiting  recreational 
disturbance to Woodwalton Fen which is a designated nature conservation site.   
 
Protecting  and  enhancing  the rights  of  ways  and  paths would  contribute  to  the  health  and 
enjoyment of the local community. 
 
The implications of flood risk should be considered in all aspects of life and development.

24. Natural Environment 
 
24.1 Most  of  the parish  of Ramsey is rural  and contains  substantial  areas  of  farmland  which 
contributes  significantly  to  the  character  of  the parish  and  the  setting  of  the town  and 
villages.  
 
24.2 There is a need to assess the likelihood of proposals or policies within a Neighbourhood Plan 
having a significant effect on the ‘National Sites Network’ consisting of areas designated as 
Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) or Special Protection Areas (SPA’s). Consideration of the 
internationally designated Ramsar sites is also necessary; many Ramsar sites are also SACs 
or  SPAs. In  the  vicinity  of the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  the ‘National Sites Network’ of 
interest  are  the Orton  Pit  SAC  (Peterborough); Nene  Washes  SPA/Ramsar (East  of 
Peterborough);   Ouse   Washes   SAC/SPA/Ramsar (North-west   of   Ely);   Portholme   SAC 
(Huntingdon/Godmanchester); and Fenland SAC/Woodwalton Fen Ramsar.  
 
24.3 The  closest  to  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area is  the Fenland  SAC/Woodwalton  Fen  Ramsar 
which immediately abuts the south-west corner of the parish near Ramsey Heights.  
 
24.4 SACs  were  previously  classified  in  accordance  with  EC  Directive  92/43/EEC  on  the 
conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (the Habitats Directive). Article 
3  of  this  Directive  requires  the  establishment  of  a  European  network  of  important high‐
quality  conservation  sites  that  will  make  a  significant  contribution  to  conserving  the  189 
habitat types and 788 species identified in Annexes I and II of the Directive. These sites are 
now  designated  under  the  Conservation  of  Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  (as 
amended). 
 
24.5 SPAs  were  sites  first  classified  in  accordance  with  Article  4  of  the  EC  Directive  on  the 
conservation of wild birds (79/409/EEC), more commonly known as the Birds Directive. They 
were classified for rare and vulnerable birds, listed in Annex I to the Birds Directive, and for 
regularly occurring migratory species. These SPA sites are now designated under the Wildlife

26.4 SuDS   are   an   approach   to   managing 
surface  water  run-off  which  seeks  to 
mimic  natural  drainage  systems  and 
retain  water  on  or  near  the  site  as 
opposed     to     traditional     drainage 
approaches which involve piping water 
off  site  as  quickly  as  possible.  SuDS 
offer    significant    advantages    over 
conventional piped drainage systems in 
reducing  flood  risk  by  attenuating  the 
rate and quantity of surface water run-
off from a site, promoting groundwater 
recharge, and improving water quality, 
biodiversity and amenity. The LLFA would particularly support above-ground open SuDS such 
as wetlands, attenuation basins, ponds and swales as they provide additional amenity and 
biodiversity benefits.

undeveloped  area  between  the  Drain  and  Hollow  Road.  Over  time  a  small  part  seems  to  have

In  relation  to  the  call  for  sites  exercise  undertaken  by  Huntingdonshire  DC  for  the  Local  Plan 
Review, the Middle Level Commissioners have suggested the land to be suitable for natural, green 
or open spaces; and land to safeguard against flooding. In the emerging Local Plan Update to 2046 
it is proposed to allocate the land for leisure moorings and open space uses. This is not inconsistent 
with  Local  Green  Space  Designation  and  for  the  avoidance  of  any  doubt the  improvement  of 
moorings and associated built infrastructure would be acceptable. 
 
As part of their plans for  future navigation, the Middle Level Commissioners would like to turn 
Ramsey Forty Foot rural mooring into a permanent mooring; however, they may need partnership 
funding to make this happen. 
 
It has historic significance as part of the waterway drainage network. The watercourse was cut 
c1651 under the direction of Vermuyden from the River Nene (old course) at Wells Bridge near 
Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Mere to Welches Dam Lock where it joins the Counter Drain (later 
the Old Bedford River), a total of 9½ miles (17km). 
 
The waterway has a natural beauty although further enhancement of the mooring would improve 
the function and overall recreational purpose without harming the overall beauty of this area. The 
mooring supports recreational use of Forty Foot as a navigable waterway and provides a modern 
recreational gateway into the village which could be developed further. The Local Green Space 
designation is not intended to prevent the mooring being replaced, improved or extended, to the 
contrary this would be supported as being complementary to its designation as Local Green Space. 
 
The  waterway  and  its  banks  provide  an  important  contribution  to  wildlife  richness,  in  an  area 
which  has  over  time  become  quite  densely  developed.  The  nature  of  the  mooring  provides  an 
opportunity for peace and tranquillity.

Theme – Infrastructure 
 
Community Aspirations 
 
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For 
the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations: 
 
Transport & Parking 
 
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads 
being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored. 
 
The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to 
navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be 
exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in 
mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway. 
 
Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having 
sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the 
town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public 
electric vehicle charging also need to be explored. 
 
Accessibility/Connectivity 
 
Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. 
The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet 
connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, 
district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify 
their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. 
Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.  
 
Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support 
for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the 
local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the 
public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units 
as well as shops is important. 
 
Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an 
important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars 
to provide connection to the larger towns and cities. 
 
We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers 
and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, 
new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking 
and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages 
and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more 
appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

Policy 8 – Sustainable Transport 
 
 
Development proposals will be supported where they demonstrate how opportunities for the use 
of sustainable modes of transport are maximised.  This should be achieved through maximising the 
potential  for  cycling  and  walking  throughout  the  site;  provision  of  safe  crossings; secure  cycle

and  existing  parts  of Ramsey and  further  afield  including Bury  and  Upwood  Airfield.  Where  a 
proposal  will  have  a  significant  impact  on  the  existing  transport  network  this  would  be  best 
demonstrated through a transport assessment. 
 
Development proposals should include recreational routes for pedestrians which link into existing 
and proposed green infrastructure in order to contribute to health and well-being. 
 
In  all  proposals  consideration  should  be  given  to  how  the  development  can  contribute to the

facilities in the town or village as relevant. 
 
Major development proposals should demonstrate how they ensure accessibility to existing public 
transport and community transport provision. Development proposals will be supported where, as 
appropriate,  they  secure  improvements to  public  transport  provision such  as  waiting  facilities, 
raised kerbs, signage and real time information systems.

Policy 9 – Highway Impact 
 
 
Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. 
Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be 
sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts 
associated with the development.  
 
Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new 
highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria:  
• Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); 
• Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and 
• Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development. 
 
Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the 
curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development 
proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on-
street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets 
would be supported. 
 
New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of 
refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily 
accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative 
methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities 
allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and 
waste management for the benefit of the community. 
 
 
32. Rights of Way Network 
 
32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that 
it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the 
parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of 
way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey 
Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no 
public rights of way.  
 
32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for 
recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use 
makes an important contribution to health and well-being. 
The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main 
services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way 
network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the 
opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. 
The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the 
rights of way network.  
 
32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the 
lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of 
footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the 
town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular 
example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the 
feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review 
 
34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to 
check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives 
and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored 
by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and 
objectives of the Plan are not being met.  
 
34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; 
Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the 
Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and 
proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning 
application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish 
Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any 
issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual 
planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments 
on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point. 
 
34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely 
that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan 
period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046. 
 
34.4 There are  a  number  of circumstances  under  which  a  partial  review  of  the  plan  may  be 
necessary, in accordance with best practice, the Town Council and its partners will consider 
undertaking a partial review of the Neighbourhood Plan no later than 5 years following its 
finalisation.

Amenity *: A positive element or elements that contribute to the overall character or enjoyment 
of an area. For example, open land, trees, historic buildings and the inter-relationship between 
them, or less tangible factors such as tranquillity. 
 
Ancient Woodland: An area that has been wooded continuously since at least 1600 AD. It includes 
ancient semi-natural woodland and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS). 
 
Conservation (for heritage policy): The process of maintaining and managing change to a heritage 
asset in a way that sustains and, where appropriate, enhances its significance. 
 
Community  Infrastructure  Levy (CIL) *:  A  levy  allowing  local  authorities  to  raise  funds  from 
owners or developers of land undertaking new building projects in their area. 
 
Development plan: Is defined in section 38 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, 
and includes adopted local plans, neighbourhood plans that have been made and published spatial 
development  strategies,  together  with  any  regional  strategy  policies  that  remain  in  force. 
Neighbourhood plans that have been approved at referendum are also part of the development 
plan, unless the local planning authority decides that the neighbourhood plan should not be made.  
 
Economic development *: Development, including those within the B and E Use Classes, public 
and community uses, and main town centre uses (but excluding housing development). 
 
Green  infrastructure: A  network  of  multi-functional  green  and  blue  spaces  and  other  natural 
features, urban and rural, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental, economic, 
health and wellbeing benefits for nature, climate, local and wider communities and prosperity.  
 
Heritage asset: A building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree 
of  significance  meriting  consideration  in  planning  decisions,  because  of  its  heritage  interest. 
Heritage  asset  includes  designated  heritage  assets  and  assets  identified  by the  local  planning 
authority (including local listing). 
 
Historic  environment:  All  aspects  of  the  environment  resulting  from  the  interaction  between 
people and places through time, including all surviving physical remains of past human activity, 
whether visible, buried or submerged, and landscaped and planted or managed flora. 
 
International,  national  and  locally  designated  sites  of  importance  for  biodiversity:  All 
international  sites  (Special  Areas of Conservation,  Special Protection  Areas,  and Ramsar  sites),

advice  produced  by  the  Government  to  inform  the  making  of  Development  Plans  including 
Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications. 
 
Ramsar  sites:  Wetlands  of  international  importance,  designated  under  the  1971 Ramsar 
Convention. 
 
Rural exception sites: Small sites used for affordable housing in perpetuity where sites would 
not normally be used for housing. Rural exception sites seek to address the needs of the local 
community by accommodating households who are either current residents or have an existing 
family or employment connection. A proportion of market homes may be allowed on the site at 
the local planning authority’s discretion, for example where essential to enable the delivery of 
affordable units without grant funding. [Also see Policy LP 28 of the Local Plan] 
 
Scheduled Monument *: Those monuments that are given legal protection by being scheduled by 
Historic England.

99 
 
Self-build and custom-build housing:  Housing built by an individual,  a group of individuals, or 
persons working with or for them, to be occupied by that individual. Such housing can be either 
market or  affordable housing. A legal definition, for  the purpose of applying the Self-build and 
Custom Housebuilding Act 2015 (as amended), is contained in section 1(A1) and (A2) of that Act. 
 
Setting of a heritage asset: The surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent 
is not fixed and may change as the asset and its surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may 
make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to 
appreciate that significance or may be neutral. 
 
Settlement  Boundary *: The  boundary  drawn  around  various  towns  and  villages  to  limit  new 
development and define the ‘built-up area’ of the settlement. Outside of the settlement boundary 
is considered to be the countryside. 
 
Significance (for heritage policy): The value of a heritage asset to this and future generations 
because  of  its  heritage  interest.  The  interest  may  be  archaeological,  architectural,  artistic  or 
historic. Significance derives not only from a heritage asset’s physical presence, but also from its 
setting.  For  World  Heritage  Sites,  the  cultural value described within each site’s Statement of 
Outstanding Universal Value forms part of its significance. 
 
Special  Areas  of  Conservation  (SAC):  Areas  defined  by  regulation  3  of  the  Conservation  of 
Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  given  special  protection  as  important 
conservation sites. 
 
Special  Protection  Areas  (SPA):  Areas  classified  under  regulation  15  of  the  Conservation  of 
Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  identified  as  being  of  international 
importance for the breeding, feeding, wintering or the migration of rare and vulnerable species 
of birds. 
 
Site  of  Special Scientific  Interest:  Sites designated  by  Natural  England  under  the  Wildlife  and 
Countryside Act 1981. 
 
Strategic Environmental Assessment: A procedure (set out in the Environmental Assessment of 
Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004) which requires the formal environmental assessment of 
certain plans and programmes which are likely to have significant effects on the environment. 
 
Supplementary planning documents: Documents which add further detail to the policies in the 
Local Plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on 
particular  issues,  such  as  design.  Supplementary  planning  documents  are  capable  of  being  a 
material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan. 
 
Sustainable transport modes: Any efficient, safe and accessible means of transport with overall 
low  impact  on  the  environment,  including  walking  and  cycling,  low  and  ultra-low  emission 
vehicles, car sharing and public transport. 
 
Windfall sites: Sites not specifically identified in the development plan.

8 Foreword

On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, welcome to the Neighbourhood Plan for our Parish area which covers  the  settlements  of Ramsey;  Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small part of Pondersbridge.

The Neighbourhood Plan sets out the vision, objectives and policies to ensure that the town and the villages maintain their character, appearance and uniqueness over the period up to 2046; whilst helping to facilitate growth. The town is undergoing significant planned development, and the Neighbourhood Plan aims to ensure that the  planned  growth  respects  the  important  features  that  make our  communities distinctive.
The Neighbourhood Plan seeks to protect and enhance the natural and built environment of the parish which forms the character of where we live.

The Neighbourhood Plan has been drawn up by a Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group on behalf of Ramsey Town Council which is the designated body for the plan area and provided the funding and support  to  enable  the  plan  to  go  ahead. The Neighbourhood Plan  has  gone through  a  number  of stages including statutory public consultation and an Independent  Examination. The  Neighbourhood  Plan was  found  to  be  appropriate  by  the  Independent Examiner who published their report in late August 2026.

The   process now involves a   local   referendum requiring a majority ‘Yes’ vote of all those voting in the referendum for it to be accepted. In the event of a ‘Yes’ vote, Huntingdonshire District Council will proceed to ‘make’ the Neighbourhood Plan for the Parish of Ramsey.

The  Neighbourhood  Plan  sets  down  a  series  of planning    policies    which    will    form    part    of Huntingdonshire’s  wider  statutory  development plan.  The  Neighbourhood  Plan will  be  used  for determining   planning   applications   alongside the Huntingdonshire Local Plan.
It  is  intended  that  the  policies  will  be  reviewed periodically to monitor the cumulative effects of the policies  and,  if  necessary,  make  changes  to  keep them up to date and relevant.
So, our personal thanks to all those who have driven the process so far and thank you for taking the time to consider the Neighbourhood Plan.
Councillor Mrs Val Fendley Mayor of Ramsey Town Council
Sarah Mullineux Lead of the Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group

9 Introduction
1. Background

1.1 The Localism Act 2011 introduced a new type of Community Led Plan.  Communities now have the right to produce a Neighbourhood Plan, setting out policies on the development and use of land.  Developing a Neighbourhood Plan is a way for communities to play a greater role in determining the future of their area. A plan period of 2046 has been chosen to match the plan period of the emerging Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2046.

1.2 The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan forms part of the statutory Development Plan. This means that Huntingdonshire District Council will determine planning applications within the Parish in accordance with the development plan which includes this Neighbourhood Plan unless material planning considerations indicate otherwise (see section 38(6) 1 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004).

1.3 This Neighbourhood Plan is a Community Led Plan.  It has been  prepared  by a  Steering  Group  made  up  of local residents and councillors on behalf of the Town Council with professional   support.   It   has   been   informed   by   public participation and consultation firstly carried out informally in    2025 with    the    local    community. The    formal Neighbourhood  Plan  preparation  process will involve  two statutory  periods  of  public  consultation;  this  is  the  first statutory consultation to undertaken in 2026 as prescribed in Regulations 2 .

1.4 A Neighbourhood Plan is a planning document and is about the use and development of land. Neighbourhood planning gives communities more control over the future of their area by giving local people the chance to have their say on what happens where they live.

1.5 A neighbourhood   plan   can   establish   general   planning policies for  the development and use of land in a particular area. Plans can include local priorities, planning policies, proposals for improving an area or providing new facilities or infrastructure and allocation of key sites for development.

1.6 Neighbourhood planning  is  a  tool  to  promote  sustainable  growth  and  will  not  be  able  to prevent  development  in  an  area.  Neighbourhood  plans  can  only  include  proposals  for  an equal  (or  greater)  amount  of  growth  than  is  set  out  in  the  local  authority's  development plan. They must also accord with national planning policy
2. Sustainability Appraisal (SA) and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)

2.1 Every Neighbourhood  Plan  needs  to  consider  the  need  for  a  Sustainability  Appraisal (incorporating a Strategic Environmental Assessment) for the Neighbourhood Plan.  SA is a mechanism  for  considering  and  communicating  the  impacts  of  an  emerging  plan,  and potential alternatives in terms of key sustainability issues.
