3. National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF)

3.1 Throughout this  Neighbourhood  Plan  reference  is  made  to  the  National  Planning  Policy Framework (NPPF).  The NPPF sets out the government’s planning policies for England and how these are expected to be applied.  It was first published on 27 March 2012, with the NPPF version 3 against  which  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  was produced  and  examined being published in December 2024. It is also supplemented by Planning Practice Guidance.
3.2 The NPPF provides a framework to produce locally distinctive Neighbourhood Plans which reflect the needs and aspirations of the community.

3.3 The Government had consulted on a new draft NPPF 4 over the period from December 2025 to March 2026. The draft NPPF proposed for the first time there is a clear set of separate policies  for  both  plan-making  and  decision-making.  This  is  intended  to  achieve  three principal objectives, namely to:

• Ensure national planning policy is accessible and understandable for  everyone who uses it; • Establish  a  comprehensive  suite  of  national  policies  on  general  planning  matters which  will  apply  across  the  country,  to  avoid  these  matters  being  repeated  or deviated from in locally-produced plans; and • Make  the  policy  which  it  contains  more  ‘rules-based’  and  certain,  and  so  more capable of supporting timely and consistent.

3.4 The Neighbourhood Plan preparation did take account of the new draft NPPF as it gave a clear direction of travel. The Government then published the new NPPF 5 in mid-August 2026 shortly before  the  Independent  Examination  of  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  ended. The Government has incorporated policies  relating  to  traveller  sites, previously set  out  in Planning Policy for Traveller Sites, within the relevant chapters of the NPPF.

3.5 The Neighbourhood Plan contributes towards the achievement of sustainable development. More detail on the ways in which this Plan addresses sustainable development is included within the Basic Conditions Statement that accompanies the Plan.
4. Planning Practice Guidance

4.1 Planning Practice  Guidance 6 sets  out  the  government’s  advice  on  how  to  undertake neighbourhood planning within England. This is set out in detail within Section 41 of Planning Practice Guidance. Planning Practice Guidance also sets out national advice on a wide range of planning topics.

7. Relationship to Huntingdonshire Local Plan

7.2 The purpose of the Local Plan is to set out: • the strategy for development in the whole of Huntingdonshire; • policies for managing development; and • details of sites for development to meet the needs of Huntingdonshire.

7.3 The District Council is in the process of undertaking a Local Plan Update 8 to be known as the Huntingdonshire Local  Plan  to  2046.  The Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  to  2046 was published for consultation during November and December 2025. There is no obligation for a Neighbourhood Plan to be in general conformity with an emerging Local Plan; although it is sensible to look to ensure that inconsistency is avoided. Although, there is no certainty that  allocations  or  proposals  identified  in  the  Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  will  be carried forward into the later stages.

7.4 In broad terms the Preferred Options Draft Local Plan to 2046 9 looked to continue the same approach  to  the  settlement hierarchy.  Limited  additional  allocations for  housing  and employment are proposed at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the north-eastern  and south-eastern sides  of  Ramsey  town. A  that  time  there were  two  main areas of consistency that need to be considered in the context of future general conformity between the emerging Neighbourhood Plan and the emerging Local Plan Review. These were in relation to a protected settlement break between Ramsey and Upwood Airfield/Bury, and the area between Ramsey Rural Museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp which the Neighbourhood Plan proposes as Local Green Space.

7.5 Any  reference  in  this  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  ‘Local  Plan Update’  means  the emerging Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2046. 7.6 The Proposed Submission Local Plan Update to 2046 still proposes allocations for housing and employment at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the south-eastern side  of  Ramsey  town. Together  with  a  housing  allocation  at  Ramsey  Forty  Foot on  the southern side.
7.7 Even if the proposed Local Government Reorganisation occurs, the Local Plan Update would still be likely to be completed by the new Council if appropriate.

The Communities of Ramsey

13.1 The Parish covers an area of 6,361 hectares. The Parish of Ramsey comprises the distinct communities of Ramsey; Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small part of Pondersbridge.

13.2 The town is the largest settlement and is  about 14 miles  (22 km)  north  of Huntingdon. The town of Ramsey grew up    around    Ramsey    Abbey,    an important  Benedictine  monastery. The  town manor is built on the site of (and using materials from) the ancient Abbey and is  the  seat  of  the  Lords  de  Ramsey, major  landowners  in  Lincolnshire  and Cambridgeshire.  The  remains  of  the Abbey  are  now  home  to  part  of  the town's secondary school.

13.3 The     Ramsey Conservation     Area Character Assessment 19 describes  the historical development of the town of Ramsey. The villages  in  Ramsey have their  origins  as  agricultural  settlements,  with  growth often  connected  to  the  land  being drained. The mid-year ONS 2024 population estimate for the Parish of Ramsey is 9,349, living in 3,819 households 20 .

18 Vision
16.1 The following vision has been developed for the Neighbourhood Plan:

To  provide  a  planning  framework  and  policies  that  will result  in  sustainable  growth  for  the  local  community, ensuring  that  appropriate  infrastructure,  services  and facilities are provided whilst also conserving the distinct character of the town and villages that form the overall community of Ramsey.
Objectives
16.2 The following objectives have been set out for the Neighbourhood Plan:
(A) Promote sustainable development and infrastructure

• Collaborate through the production of development plans and the determination of planning applications  including  pre-application  engagement with  Huntingdonshire District  Council and  developers  of  individual  parcels to ensure  that growth  of  the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area delivers sustainable growth without resulting in further coalescence with Bury and Upwood Airfield. • Ensure that new development is of high-quality design, is built to a high sustainability standard and includes or contributes to open space and community facilities. • Ensure that the design and location of new development is resilient to the effects of climate change and flooding. • Ensure that new development integrates into the existing town or village including linking  all  developments  to  the  rest  of  the town  or village  with  footpaths,  where appropriate. • Locate new development such that current problems with congestion, parking and road safety are not exacerbated and, if possible, reduced.
(B) Conserve and enhance the built and natural environment

• Protect, enhance and conserve the open spaces; landscape; views; and biodiversity across the town and villages. • Use land efficiently and to preserve high quality agricultural land. • Conserve  and  enhance  the built environment  of  the town  and villages, including through  ensuring that  new  development  respects  or  enhances  the distinctive character and appearance of the area in which it is sited.
(C) Protect and develop the communities of Ramsey

• Protect  and  preserve  important community assets  including  its  local  services  and facilities by encouraging the retention and growth of community facilities. • Continue to improve the facilities on offer to support the local community, including through outreach services. • Continue to support community events.

Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Community, the following are the community aspirations:
Community

The Town  Council  and  Neighbourhood Plan  want  to  support the  various  communities  that collectively  make  up  the  parish  of  Ramsey. A  vibrant  and flourishing community includes supporting families; encouraging the provision of places to live, work, stay and play; with suitable provision of housing including a local connection for housing and affordable housing.

The communities of Ramsey need suitable resilience to adapt to changing circumstances and be supported  to  allow  suitable  access  to  services  and  facilities  despite  the  relative  geographic isolation.

Resilience also needs to cater for ageing population needs; this includes the provision of specialist supported accommodation such as extra care housing or supported living schemes for people of all ages with care and support needs. Provision of adult mental health supported accommodation and  provision  for  adults  with  learning  disabilities  needs  to  be  provided  as  part  of  an  overall balanced and mixed community.
It is an aspiration to ensure that community clubs for  all ages are available and that access to adult education is available locally.

Adequate provision of services in proportion to the growth is imperative.  Additional services or replacement or extension of existing community buildings such as the library, community centre needs  to  be  factored  in. The  communities  want  a  holistic  and  joined  up  approach  so  that development,  infrastructure  and services  are  set  up  in  a  harmonious,  cohesive  and  sustainable way.
Education
Education needs to be fit for purpose and be well located; including being accessible safely for all ages by active travel methods including by foot and bicycle.

Suitable  and  adequate  early  years  provision to  meet  the  differing  needs  of  families.  Such  as through day nurseries, full day care, sessional provisional, childminders and wraparound care to provide breakfast and after school provision term-time between the hours of 8am and 6pm; need to be available in order to allow parents the opportunity to return to work. Additional capacity is required across  schools to meet demand. In terms of wider education, access to adult education should be available locally.

19. Definition of ‘Built-up Area’ (Settlement Boundary)

19.1 Ramsey town has planned strategic  growth on sites allocated in the Local Plan. However, there has been pressure  for planning  applications to come forward  for  residential development on greenfield sites which are not allocated. Such speculative development in addition to the allocated sites has the potential to undermine the strategic policies of the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 in terms of the distribution of housing across the district. It also has the potential to affect the distinctive character and separate identity of Ramsey and the adjacent village of Bury as separate and distinct settlements.

19.2 Ramsey  town is part of the ‘Ramsey Spatial Planning Area’ in Policy LP 2 - Strategy  for Development.  Policy  LP  7 - Spatial  Planning  Areas,  supports  development  where  it  is appropriately  located  within  a  built-up  area  of  an  identified  Spatial  Planning  Area settlement. The Local Plan does not specify any specific housing requirement for the villages of Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; nor for  the
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)

31 part of Pondersbridge which are all deemed as ‘small settlements’ in the Local Plan. There is an overall allowance for windfall development to come forward across the collective 73 small settlements in the Local Plan.

19.3 The Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 does not identify a settlement boundary for these villages; instead, it  moves  to  use  of a definition of ‘built-up area’. Policy  LP 9 – Small Settlements, supports development where it is appropriately located within a built-up area of a small settlement. This is what is known as windfall development as it relates to housing coming forward on sites not specifically allocated for housing.

19.4 A settlement boundary is proposed for the town of Ramsey. As this will be contiguous with the  built-up  area  of  the  adjoining  village  of  Bury in  some  places;  as  explained in the Settlement  Boundary  Methodology document we have  ensured that  consistency  with  the settlement  boundary  in  the  Bury Neighbourhood Plan has  taken place.

19.5 For Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & Ramsey  St  Mary’s a settlement  boundary  is proposed  to  be identified to  define  the  ‘built-up  area’ as  referred  to  in  the Huntingdonshire   Local   Plan   to   2036. The   small   part   of Pondersbridge  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  on  its  own  falls below  the  size  parameter  of  30  homes  in  the  Local  Plan  to  be identified  as  a  built-up  area. Therefore,  as  explained  in  the Settlement   Boundary   Methodology document,   no   settlement boundary   for   Pondersbridge   has been established   in   the Neighbourhood Plan.

19.6 The settlement boundary  of these  settlements serves a  specific purpose  in  that  it  is  intended  to direct the  growth  of  the settlement and  enable development  to  take  place  in  a  coherent manner,  maintaining  the  structure  and  form  of  the  existing  settlement  geography as  the Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036 envisages.  In  addition,  the  boundary  will  protect  the landscape setting of the villages.

19.7 The Huntingdonshire Townscape SPD for Ramsey identifies wording that says, ‘Reflect the existing built forms and local relationship with the street in any new development’. Policy 1 of the NP refers to taking into account the existing built form, layout and structure of the surrounding area.

19.8 This is intended to cover the wide array of factors that contribute to the distinctiveness of how a place looks, works and functions. In terms of structure, we mean factors such as the configuration,  the    arrangement  of  the  built  elements  in  a  particular  form,  figure,  or combination.

19.9 The National Design Guide suggests that structure can be a separate consideration to built form or layout.  For  example,  M2 of National Design Guide looks for  a clear structure and hierarchy of streets. It goes on to identify in relation to Layout that: “A layout shows how routes and blocks of development are arranged and relate to one another to create streets, open spaces and buildings. It defines: the structure or settlement pattern; the grain, or the pattern of development blocks and plots; and the broad distribution of different uses, and their densities or building heights.”
19.10 The National Design Guide also refers to the structure of blocks and routes that this creates; as well as open space, its location and structure need careful consideration.

20.1 Parts of Bury immediately abut the town of Ramsey, together with Upwood Airfield the two settlements form the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area. 20.2 The Parish boundary between Bury and Ramsey was established before much of the growth and development occurred. Over time a degree of coalescence between Bury and Ramsey has already occurred. The northern part of Bury around Signal Road is contiguous with the main  part  of  Ramsey,  as  such  although  spatially  part  of  Bury, it  physically  and  visually appears  as  an  extension  to  Ramsey.  The  two  settlements  are  however  two  distinct communities and are in two separate but contiguous Parishes.

20.2 The inter-relationship between Ramsey and Bury can be considered in relation to the two broad areas of: 1. East of the B1040; and 2. West of the B1040. As the B1040 for part of its length  forms  the Parish  boundary on  the  north-south  alignment,  this  provides  a  logical feature to choose as the central point to work from in order to undertake an assessment.

20.4 East of the B1040 - There are in fact no gaps remaining between the two Parishes of Ramsey and Bury to the east of the B1040. However, there is a gap between the northern part of Bury around Signal Road and the main part of Bury village. This remaining gap is the only visual and physical separation between the main cores of Bury and Ramsey. Consequently, the Bury Neighbourhood Plan has identified this as a Protected Settlement Break as the only gap remaining to prevent the complete coalescence of Ramsey and Bury.

Ramsey  has  grown,  including  through  the  recent development of Frost Way and Stonemason Way. This recent housing development has led to the greater threat of coalescence on the western side between Ramsey, Bury and Upwood Airfield. There is a wedge of countryside remaining between the northern side of Upwood Airfield,  the  western  side  of  Longland  Crescent  and  the  southern  side  of housing  on  the south-western fringe of the town of Ramsey.

20.7 Given  that  the  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  proposes  that  the  ‘Ramsey  Spatial Planning Area’ has allocations for 895 homes and 2 hectares of employment land there is a real threat that unchecked growth could lead to further coalescence between Ramsey and Bury.  The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  does  not  include  any policy  to prevent  the coalescence of Ramsey and Bury, although the Bury Neighbourhood Plan does. In terms of consistency,  it  is  appropriate  for  the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  also  secure  this important community objective of retaining the distinct settlements of Ramsey and Bury.

20.8 There  is  also  the  potential  through  further  urban  extension  for  development  on  Upwood Airfield to lead to coalescence on the western side between Ramsey and Bury. The allocations at Upwood Airfield  as  a  whole  visually  and  spatially appears  to  be part  of  Bury.  The  northern side  of  the  Airfield  in  this  area  is  rather distinctively  formed by  the  former  runway and  the  hedgerow  and  treed  boundary.  To the   north   of   this   is   a   wedge-shaped agricultural  field  that  currently  provides  a visual  and  physical  separation  in  the  built form between  Ramsey and Bury including Upwood  Airfield.  The  area  has  a  width  of around  130m  at  its  eastern  end  rising  to around 230m at the western end.

Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Heritage & Environment, the following are the community aspirations:
Heritage & Tourism

The parish is home to a wealth of heritage assets, and the historic environment has been identified through public consultation as being of particular importance to local residents. Specifically, it is a community aspiration to ensure that the heritage is adequately protected and supported. Events and assets such as the rural museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp are important both to the heritage of the area and the tourism offer.
Potential linkages to proposed major tourism provision at Bedford should be considered to see how the wider sub region can benefit from tourism investment and visitors.

In order to protect the heritage of the area, protection of areas like Stocking Fen and the area north  of  Tesco should  be  secured. Retaining  Ramsey  and  Bury  as distinct  settlements  is fundamental to the history of Ramsey; so, protecting a gap between Bury and Ramsey through maintaining a settlement break is a significant community aspiration.
The agricultural origins of the parish are a fundamental part of the character of the area. The preservation of agriculture and the agricultural heritage and culture is therefore important.
Great Fen & Biodiversity
The Great Fen project extends into Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s, linkages to the Great Fen waterways plan and visitor centre is important.

The  biodiversity of  the  area and the protection  of  green  spaces is  important  to  allow  the communities  to enjoy  the  outside  for  recreation  and  views;  whilst  limiting  recreational disturbance to Woodwalton Fen which is a designated nature conservation site.
Protecting  and  enhancing  the rights  of  ways  and  paths would  contribute  to  the  health  and enjoyment of the local community.
The implications of flood risk should be considered in all aspects of life and development.

23.3 Areas of special architectural or  historic interest are designated as Conservation Areas to help   preserve   and   enhance   them   for   future generations. 24. Natural Environment

24.1 Most  of  the parish  of Ramsey is rural  and contains  substantial  areas  of  farmland  which contributes  significantly  to  the  character  of  the parish  and  the  setting  of  the town  and villages.

24.2 There is a need to assess the likelihood of proposals or policies within a Neighbourhood Plan having a significant effect on the ‘National Sites Network’ consisting of areas designated as Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) or Special Protection Areas (SPA’s). Consideration of the internationally designated Ramsar sites is also necessary; many Ramsar sites are also SACs or  SPAs. In  the  vicinity  of the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  the ‘National Sites Network’ of interest  are  the Orton  Pit  SAC  (Peterborough); Nene  Washes  SPA/Ramsar (East  of Peterborough);   Ouse   Washes   SAC/SPA/Ramsar (North-west   of   Ely);   Portholme   SAC (Huntingdon/Godmanchester); and Fenland SAC/Woodwalton Fen Ramsar.
24.3 The  closest  to  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area is  the Fenland  SAC/Woodwalton  Fen  Ramsar which immediately abuts the south-west corner of the parish near Ramsey Heights.

24.4 SACs  were  previously  classified  in  accordance  with  EC  Directive  92/43/EEC  on  the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (the Habitats Directive). Article 3  of  this  Directive  requires  the  establishment  of  a  European  network  of  important high‐ quality  conservation  sites  that  will  make  a  significant  contribution  to  conserving  the  189 habitat types and 788 species identified in Annexes I and II of the Directive. These sites are now  designated  under  the  Conservation  of  Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  (as amended).

24.5 SPAs  were  sites  first  classified  in  accordance  with  Article  4  of  the  EC  Directive  on  the conservation of wild birds (79/409/EEC), more commonly known as the Birds Directive. They were classified for rare and vulnerable birds, listed in Annex I to the Birds Directive, and for regularly occurring migratory species. These SPA sites are now designated under the Wildlife
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
60 &  Countryside  Act  1981  (as  amended)  and  the  Conservation  (Natural  Habitats,  &  c.) Regulations 2010 (as amended).

24.6 Ramsar Sites are designated under the International Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (the Ramsar Convention, Iran 1971 and amended by  the  Paris  Protocol  1992).  Although Ramsar  Sites are not protected in law by domestic  UK  legislation  as  a  matter  of policy   government, has   decreed   that unless   otherwise   specified   procedures relating  to  SPAs  and  SACs  will  also  apply to Ramsar Sites.

24.7 The    Habitats    Regulation    Assessment screening identifies that the Neighbourhood  Plan  proposals  would  not individually  or  cumulatively  result  in  any potential    significant    effects    on    any designated site.

24.8 The plan area contains no National Nature Reserves (NNR), Woodwalton Fen is also a NNR in addition to being a SAC and Ramsar  site. The other nearest NNR are at Upwood Meadows around 2km to the south-west and Holme Fen around 2km to the west of Ramsey St Mary’s. The Plan area contains no Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Woodwalton Fen is also a SSSI in addition to being an NNR, SAC and Ramsar site; Holme Fen is also a SSSI as well as being an NNR. Warboys  and  Wistow  Woods  SSSI  lies around  3km  to  the  south  of  Ramsey (town).

24.9 There are impact zones defined around the various designated sites to identify what scale of different types of development need consultation with Natural England. This principally impacts  on  Ramsey  Heights  and  Ramsey  St  Mary’s,  although  the  impact  zones  do  extend further across the Parish. These impact zones are shown in Appendix 1.

24.10 In  terms  of County  level  locally  designated  sites (County  Wildlife  Sites),  the  plan  area contains Ramsey Heights Nature Reserve and Reservoir East of Park Farm which lies north- east of Ramsey towards Ramsey Hollow.

24.11 The Great Fen Project Area extends into the western part of the parish near Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s. The Great Fen Landscape & Visual Setting boundary extends across the western part of the parish, covering land west of Ugg Mere Court Road in Ramsey Heights and west of the B1040 in Ramsey St Mary’s.

24.12 The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS 44 ) is a bold new plan to revive and protect nature across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. It’s a locally driven, government-backed initiative that maps out where and how we can restore habitats, boost biodiversity, and reconnect people with the natural world, from countryside to city parks.

26.2 Surface  water  flooding  potential  affects  much  of  the  parish  of  Ramsey.  Surface  water flooding  is  a  matter  to  be  taken  into  account  in  the  planning  application  process 49 . The Neighbourhood Plan alongside the Local Plan and the NPPF strives to promote sustainable drainage techniques (SuDS).

26.3 Fluvial (river) flooding and surface water flooding risks change over  time, in part at least due to the impact of climate change. Developers when designing surface water systems have to design them with an allowance for climate change 50 . During December 2020 there were a large volume of flood incidents across Cambridgeshire, Ramsey was affected. The Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA) undertook a statutory flood investigation and produced the relevant report 51 .

26.4 SuDS   are   an   approach   to   managing surface  water  run-off  which  seeks  to mimic  natural  drainage  systems  and retain  water  on  or  near  the  site  as opposed     to     traditional     drainage approaches which involve piping water off  site  as  quickly  as  possible.  SuDS offer    significant    advantages    over conventional piped drainage systems in reducing  flood  risk  by  attenuating  the rate and quantity of surface water run- off from a site, promoting groundwater recharge, and improving water quality, biodiversity and amenity. The LLFA would particularly support above-ground open SuDS such as wetlands, attenuation basins, ponds and swales as they provide additional amenity and biodiversity benefits.

26.5 Opportunities for increasing biodiversity at opportunity sites and in the protected settlement breaks are  discussed  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan. There  is  a potential  for  increasing biodiversity through the use of SuDS features such as attenuation basins, ponds and swales in these circumstances.

The area is one of the important open areas in this part of the town that forms part of the overall significance of the Conservation Area. The area is part of the Green Fringe Character Area of the Conservation Area identified in the Conservation Area Character Appraisal. As such it forms part of a network of open spaces with mature trees that give the eastern fringe part of the town a distinctive character and appearance. The field has a parkland character from the mature trees within it.

The Conservation Area Character Appraisal identifies that the Cemetery and Rural Museum form a buffer between the housing area of the town and this open land. The verdant and undeveloped nature  of  the  area  contributes  strongly  to  the  character  and  appearance  of  this  part  of  the Conservation Area.

The  land  is  abutted  on  both  sides  by  the Ramsey Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp. It  has  historical  significance  through helping  both  of  those  attractions  tell  the story of the history of the town through the various events hosted on the land.

This  space  is  an  integral  part  of  Ramsey’s heritage.  Currently, the field is used for the maximum allowable events throughout the year. It links the Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp  and  allows  for  highly  successful  joint  ventures  as  well  as  solo  events.  Without  it,  large community and nationally recognised events will no longer be able to occur causing loss of funding for both the Ramsey 1940s Camp and Ramsey Rural Museum. This could jeopardise the viability of both sites.

Historically, the side of the Museum protruding into the field was identified as an historic track and is adjacent to  what  is  believed  to  be  the  boundary  of  the  Abbey precinct 53 . There is also a possibility of ordinance from the Ramsey 1940s Camp from when it was a searchlight facility during World War II.  The area of the Camp was used during World War I, but documentation associated with  that  appears  to  be  sealed,  possibly  under  the Official Secrets Act.

The area is effectively an events space and showground where  a  significant  number  of  public  events  are  held. These  events  are  integral  to  the  cultural,  social  and  economic  life  of  the  community,  local businesses and attractions. Events held include the 1940s Weekend, the Fen Fair, Country Fair and Plough Day, Ramsey Steam & Fire Show. These events can have up to 3,500 people attending. The area is also used for other events including Dog Shows and Scooter Rallies.

The  area  of  Ramsey  Town  Moorings  on  the  High  Lode  has  been  partially  altered  through  the development The Moorings off Stocking Fen Road. It lies close to the Ramsey Community Centre and Rainbow Surgery. It is at the point where High  Lode  changes  from  being  an  open-air waterway   to   becoming   an   underground waterway   running   southwards   under  The Great  Whyte  through  the  Ramsey  Tunnels after going through the Mill Sluice.

In around 2022 some 120m of new permanent visitor  moorings  were  completed  on  the eastern  side.  These  visitor  moorings  are owned  and  maintained  by  the  Middle  Level Commissioners   and   were   made   possible following  the  change  in  focus  and  funding arising  from  the  2018  Middle  Level  Act  and the introduction of licensing. The land beyond the bank has recently transferred from the housing developer to Ramsey Town Council.

It  has  historic  significance  as  the  waterway  adjacent  to  the  Corn  Mill  now  known  as  Rivermill Apartments and as part of the nineteenth century industrial area. That character area within the Ramsey  Conservation  Area  contained  the  LNER  Holme  &  Ramsey  Branch  line  which  hosted  the North  Station,  where  North  Station  Close  is  currently  sited.  The  importance  of  the  Ramsey northern gateway goes back to Saxon times, which is the most likely time that the navigable Lodes became the chief form of commercial transport for the town.

The  waterway  has  a  natural  beauty  although  further  enhancement  of  the  public  realm  would improve the overall beauty of this gateway. The eastern side of the moorings has a modern quay; the  western  side  of  the  moorings has an older quayside. The moorings support  recreational  use  of  High Lode  as  a  navigable  waterway  and provides   a   modern   recreational gateway into the town which could be developed further.

The waterway and its banks provide an    important    contribution    to wildlife  richness,  in  an  area  which has over time become quite densely developed.    Notwithstanding    the nature of the B1040 passing by the moorings, the area still provides an opportunity for tranquillity.
Horse Drove, which is an unmade track, runs along the western side of the moorings. Its physical condition has suffered in recent years from use and could benefit from improvement.

The  area  of  Ramsey  Forty  Foot  Moorings  on  the  Forty  Foot  or  Vermuden’s  Drain  Lode  is  an undeveloped  area  between  the  Drain  and  Hollow  Road. In  relation  to  the  call  for  sites  exercise  undertaken  by  Huntingdonshire  DC  for  the  Local  Plan Review, the Middle Level Commissioners have suggested the land to be suitable for natural, green or open spaces; and land to safeguard against flooding. As part of their plans for  future navigation, the Middle Level Commissioners would like to turn Ramsey Forty Foot rural mooring into a permanent mooring; however, they may need partnership funding to make this happen.

It has historic significance as part of the waterway drainage network. The watercourse was cut c1651 under the direction of Vermuyden from the River Nene (old course) at Wells Bridge near Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Mere to Welches Dam Lock where it joins the Counter Drain (later the Old Bedford River), a total of 9½ miles (17km).

The waterway has a natural beauty although further enhancement of the mooring would improve the function and overall recreational purpose without harming the overall beauty of this area. The mooring supports recreational use of Forty Foot as a navigable waterway and provides a modern recreational gateway into the village which could be developed further. The Local Green Space designation is not intended to prevent the mooring being replaced, improved or extended, to the contrary this would be supported as being complementary to its designation as Local Green Space.

The  waterway  and  its  banks  provide  an  important  contribution  to  wildlife  richness,  in  an  area which  has  over  time  become  quite  densely  developed.  The  nature  of  the  mooring  provides  an opportunity for peace and tranquillity.

82 Theme – Infrastructure
Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations:
Transport & Parking
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored.

The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway.

Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public electric vehicle charging also need to be explored.
Accessibility/Connectivity

Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.

Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units as well as shops is important.

Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars to provide connection to the larger towns and cities.

We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

30.1 Local planning policy recognises that Ramsey and the surrounding area has relatively poor transport infrastructure, being well off the primary road network and relatively remote. Its comparatively  limited  services,  facilities  and  employment  opportunities  make  it  a  less sustainable   location   in   terms  of   travel   than   some  of   the  other   market   towns   in Cambridgeshire.

30.2 Ramsey and the surrounding villages are classed as a rural area, there are high levels of car ownership  and  reliance  on  the  car  to  maintain  access  to  key  services. Some  87.7%  of households  in  the  parish  of  Ramsey have  one or  more  cars/vans,  with almost  half  of  the households having two, three or more cars/vans. In addition, high house prices and lack of affordable housing has led to more people travelling further to work, with the average length of commute in Ramsey greater than the national average. Access to employment, education and services can be a real challenge without a car in rural areas.

30.3 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036  contains  Policy  LP  16  which indicates that new development will be  expected  to  contribute  to  an enhanced  transport  network  that supports an increasing proportion of journeys    being    undertaken    by sustainable travel modes.

30.4 Access    to    high    quality    public transport  is  known  to  be  hugely beneficial  to  improving  access  to services for  those members of society who cannot,  for a variety of reasons, access a car. This is particularly acute in rural areas such as Ramsey where distances between households and essential services are often large, making walking and cycling less practical than in urban areas. The villages in the parish are reliant upon Ramsey town for many higher order services and facilities. However, the town doesn’t provide all essential services and journeys to larger settlements  such  as  Peterborough or  Huntingdon  are  necessary,  for  example to  access hospital services, higher education and many public services. The Town Council alongside the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood Trust 64 does  look  to  support  the  provision  of  outreach public services to improve accessibility.

30.5 It  has  recently  been  announced  that  there  will  be  a  new  direct  bus  service (X31) from Upwood, Bury and Ramsey to Peterborough from January 2026. This will be operated under the new Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority contract 65 .

30.6 The geographic nature of the parish makes it difficult for residents of the villages to access the services and facilities in Ramsey town centre by walking and cycling. The distances in combination with the lack of footways and uneven road surfaces due to the fenland geology are barriers to walking and cycling.

30.7 The Vision for Ramsey document (extract overleaf) sets out a number of transport initiatives that the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority and Huntingdonshire District Council have developed.

30.8 The  Government  through  Active  Travel  England is  looking  to  make  walking,  wheeling  and cycling the preferred choice for everyone to get around in England. Active travel is the term often  used  to encompass  elements  such  as  walking  to  school,  cycling  to  work,  or  other everyday journeys you make to get from place to place, rather than just walking or cycling solely for leisure or fitness. In addition, active travel can offer a convenient, accessible and affordable way to move more for shorter journeys. National policy in the NPPF does not refer to active travel but instead refers to sustainable transport but includes that policies should look for opportunities to promote walking, cycling and public transport use are identified and  pursued.  Active  travel  and sustainable  travel  modes not  only  positively  contribute  to addressing climate change but also can assist in maintaining a healthy community.

Policy 8 – Sustainable Transport

Development proposals will be supported where they demonstrate how opportunities for the use of sustainable modes of transport are maximised.  This should be achieved through maximising the potential  for  cycling  and  walking  throughout  the  site;  provision  of  safe  crossings; secure  cycle storage in public places, workplaces and in new dwellings; and linkages through to adjacent sites and  existing  parts  of Ramsey and  further  afield  including Bury  and  Upwood  Airfield.  Where  a proposal  will  have  a  significant  impact  on  the  existing  transport  network  this  would  be  best demonstrated through a transport assessment.
Development proposals should include recreational routes for pedestrians which link into existing and proposed green infrastructure in order to contribute to health and well-being.

In  all  proposals  consideration  should  be  given  to  how  the  development  can  contribute to the delivery  of  the  provision  of  a  network  of  walking  and  cycling  linkages 70 to the key  services & facilities in the town or village as relevant.

Major development proposals should demonstrate how they ensure accessibility to existing public transport and community transport provision. Development proposals will be supported where, as appropriate,  they  secure  improvements to  public  transport  provision such  as  waiting  facilities, raised kerbs, signage and real time information systems.

31. Highway Impact

31.1 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  contains Policy  LP  16  on  Sustainable  Travel  and Policy  LP  17 on Parking Provision  and  Vehicle Movement.  This latter policy  indicates  that
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
90 proposals  must incorporate  adequate  parking  for  vehicles  and  cycles.  Advice  on  parking arrangements is contained in the Huntingdonshire Design Guide SPD (2017) 71 .

30.2 Early consultation identified a significant level of concern regarding the volume of traffic and road safety. There was also a significant level of concern about the road infrastructure and  difficulties  with parking.  Improving  road safety  would  enhance  the  quality of life of some of the most vulnerable members of the community. Unfortunately, traffic management is not an issue over which the Town Council has direct control. Most of the traffic originates outside the parish. As a consequence, traffic management cannot be easily addressed by this Neighbourhood  Plan.  However,  the Town  Council will  seek  to  support road  safety improvements around the plan area.

30.3 As part of the overall approach, the Neighbourhood Plan can support and ensure that new development  does  not  adversely  affect  the  highway  network; or  that  where  it  does, contributions through    a    Planning Obligation address     the     impacts appropriately. However, a Planning Obligation can only be sought where it meets the relevant tests; namely: it is necessary  to  make  the  development acceptable   in   planning   terms;   is directly  related  to  the  development; and is fairly and reasonably related in scale   and   kind. In   some cases, Cambridgeshire   County   Council   is seeking  more  direct  off-site  delivery of highway improvements, i.e. rather than paying the County Council a fee the  developer  will  undertake  the  works  in  the highway  directly. As such  in  some  cases  a planning  condition  may  be  the  appropriate  implementation  measure.  In  some cases, Community Infrastructure Levy monies will cover highway improvements.

30.4 The  policy  includes  reference  to the  storage  and  collection  of  refuse  bins as  where insufficient on-site provision is made this can result in a highway impact. This impact involves bins blocking pedestrian use of footways that can lead to pedestrian and vehicle conflict. The Cambridgeshire RECAP Waste Management Design Guide SPD 72 sets out advice on access, maximum travel distances, number of bins per property type etc. and takes into account the Council’s  Waste  Collection  Policies. The  policy looks  to provide  the  opportunity  for developers to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage,  for  example on larger sites if viability and operational practicalities support this approach  in  a development. Alternative  or  innovative  methods of storage could have the added benefit of improving the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community, particularly where smaller dwellings are concentrated, and the provision of wheeled bins may be less desirable.

30.5 Where parking courts are proposed, care needs to be taken. These spaces often suffer from poor  natural surveillance, limited  overlooking  and  can  become  unsafe or underused.  It  is recommended in the policy that parking courts should only be used where they are small, well-overlooked,   incorporate   high   quality   and   subtle   use   of materials,   integrated landscaping and trees. The HDC Design Guide SPD 2017 on page 89 provides more detailed advice.

Policy 9 – Highway Impact

Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts associated with the development.

Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria: • Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); • Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and • Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development.

Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on- street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets would be supported.

New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community.
32. Rights of Way Network

32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no public rights of way.

32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use makes an important contribution to health and well-being. The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the rights of way network.

32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review

34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and objectives of the Plan are not being met.

34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point.

34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046.

34.4 There are  a  number  of circumstances  under  which  a  partial  review  of  the  plan  may  be necessary, in accordance with best practice, the Town Council and its partners will consider undertaking a partial review of the Neighbourhood Plan no later than 5 years following its finalisation.

Affordable housing *: Housing for sale or rent, for those whose needs are not met by the market (including housing that provides a subsidised route to home ownership and/or is for essential local workers); and which complies with one or more of the following categories: affordable housing for rent;  starter  homes; discounted  market  sales  housing;  and  other  affordable  routes  to  home ownership including shared ownership, relevant equity loans, other low cost homes for sale (at a price equivalent to at least 20% below local market value) and rent to buy (which includes a period of intermediate rent). [Note a more detailed definition is included in the NPPF 77 ]

Amenity *: A positive element or elements that contribute to the overall character or enjoyment of an area. For example, open land, trees, historic buildings and the inter-relationship between them, or less tangible factors such as tranquillity.
Ancient Woodland: An area that has been wooded continuously since at least 1600 AD. It includes ancient semi-natural woodland and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS).
Conservation (for heritage policy): The process of maintaining and managing change to a heritage asset in a way that sustains and, where appropriate, enhances its significance.
Community  Infrastructure  Levy (CIL) *:  A  levy  allowing  local  authorities  to  raise  funds  from owners or developers of land undertaking new building projects in their area.

Development plan: Is defined in section 38 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, and includes adopted local plans, neighbourhood plans that have been made and published spatial development  strategies,  together  with  any  regional  strategy  policies  that  remain  in  force. Neighbourhood plans that have been approved at referendum are also part of the development plan, unless the local planning authority decides that the neighbourhood plan should not be made.
Economic development *: Development, including those within the B and E Use Classes, public and community uses, and main town centre uses (but excluding housing development).

Green  infrastructure: A  network  of  multi-functional  green  and  blue  spaces  and  other  natural features, urban and rural, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental, economic, health and wellbeing benefits for nature, climate, local and wider communities and prosperity.

Heritage asset: A building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree of  significance  meriting  consideration  in  planning  decisions,  because  of  its  heritage  interest. Heritage  asset  includes  designated  heritage  assets  and  assets  identified  by the  local  planning authority (including local listing).

Historic  environment:  All  aspects  of  the  environment  resulting  from  the  interaction  between people and places through time, including all surviving physical remains of past human activity, whether visible, buried or submerged, and landscaped and planted or managed flora.

International,  national  and  locally  designated  sites  of  importance  for  biodiversity:  All international  sites  (Special  Areas of Conservation,  Special Protection  Areas,  and Ramsar  sites),

98 national  sites  (Sites  of  Special  Scientific  Interest)  and  locally  designated  sites  including  Local Wildlife Sites.

Living Conditions *:  The circumstances affecting the way in which people live, especially with regard  to  their  well-being.  Relevant  factors  include:  internal  space;  access  to  external  space; outlook; privacy; daylight; sunlight; overbearing impact; impact from pollution including noise.

Local  planning  authority: The  public  authority  whose  duty  it  is  to  carry  out  specific  planning functions  for  a  particular  area.  All  references  to  local  planning  authority  include  the  district council, London borough council, county council, Broads Authority, National Park Authority, the Mayor   of   London   and   a   development   corporation,   to   the   extent   appropriate   to   their responsibilities. Local Plan: A plan for  the future development of a local area, drawn up by the local planning authority in consultation with the community. In law this is described as the development plan documents adopted under the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004. A local plan can consist of either strategic or non-strategic policies, or a combination of the two.

Neighbourhood  plans: A  plan  prepared  by  a  parish  council  or  neighbourhood  forum  for  a designated neighbourhood area. In law this is described as a neighbourhood development plan in the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004.

NPPF *: National Planning Policy Framework, this forms the overall planning policy produced by the Government to inform the making of Development Plans including Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications.

Open space: All open space of public value, including not just land, but also areas of water (such as rivers, canals, lakes and reservoirs) which offer important opportunities for sport and recreation and can act as a visual amenity.

Policies  Map *: A  document  which  illustrates  on  a  base  map  all  the  policies  and  proposals contained in this Neighbourhood Plan or another document which forms part of the Development Plan.

Planning condition: A condition imposed on a grant of planning permission (in accordance with the Town and Country Planning Act 1990) or a condition included in a Local Development Order or Neighbourhood Development Order.
Planning obligation: A legally enforceable obligation entered into under section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to mitigate the impacts of a development proposal.

Planning  Practice  Guidance  *: this  forms  the  overall  national  planning  practice  guidance  and advice  produced  by  the  Government  to  inform  the  making  of  Development  Plans  including Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications.
Ramsar  sites:  Wetlands  of  international  importance,  designated  under  the  1971 Ramsar Convention.

Rural exception sites: Small sites used for affordable housing in perpetuity where sites would not normally be used for housing. Rural exception sites seek to address the needs of the local community by accommodating households who are either current residents or have an existing family or employment connection. A proportion of market homes may be allowed on the site at the local planning authority’s discretion, for example where essential to enable the delivery of affordable units without grant funding. [Also see Policy LP 28 of the Local Plan]
Scheduled Monument *: Those monuments that are given legal protection by being scheduled by Historic England.

Self-build and custom-build housing:  Housing built by an individual,  a group of individuals, or persons working with or for them, to be occupied by that individual. Such housing can be either market or  affordable housing. A legal definition, for  the purpose of applying the Self-build and Custom Housebuilding Act 2015 (as amended), is contained in section 1(A1) and (A2) of that Act.

Setting of a heritage asset: The surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent is not fixed and may change as the asset and its surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to appreciate that significance or may be neutral.

Settlement  Boundary *: The  boundary  drawn  around  various  towns  and  villages  to  limit  new development and define the ‘built-up area’ of the settlement. Outside of the settlement boundary is considered to be the countryside.

Significance (for heritage policy): The value of a heritage asset to this and future generations because  of  its  heritage  interest.  The  interest  may  be  archaeological,  architectural,  artistic  or historic. Significance derives not only from a heritage asset’s physical presence, but also from its setting.  For  World  Heritage  Sites,  the  cultural value described within each site’s Statement of Outstanding Universal Value forms part of its significance.

Special  Areas  of  Conservation  (SAC):  Areas  defined  by  regulation  3  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  given  special  protection  as  important conservation sites.

Special  Protection  Areas  (SPA):  Areas  classified  under  regulation  15  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  identified  as  being  of  international importance for the breeding, feeding, wintering or the migration of rare and vulnerable species of birds.
Site  of  Special Scientific  Interest:  Sites designated  by  Natural  England  under  the  Wildlife  and Countryside Act 1981.

Strategic Environmental Assessment: A procedure (set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004) which requires the formal environmental assessment of certain plans and programmes which are likely to have significant effects on the environment.

Supplementary planning documents: Documents which add further detail to the policies in the Local Plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on particular  issues,  such  as  design.  Supplementary  planning  documents  are  capable  of  being  a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan.

Sustainable transport modes: Any efficient, safe and accessible means of transport with overall low  impact  on  the  environment,  including  walking  and  cycling,  low  and  ultra-low  emission vehicles, car sharing and public transport.
Windfall sites: Sites not specifically identified in the development plan.

news.title: Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version) Released
news.summary: Ramsey Town Council has published the Referendum Version of the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan for 2026-2046, detailing policies on housing, heritage, environment, and infrastructure for the parish.
news.content: Ramsey Town Council has released the Referendum Version of the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan, covering the period 2026-2046. The plan encompasses the settlements of Ramsey, Ramsey Forty Foot, Ramsey Heights, Ramsey Mereside, Ramsey St Mary's, Ramsey Hollow, and part of Pondersbridge. Produced with support from neighbourhood-plan.co.uk and guided by a steering group led by Sarah Mullineux, the document outlines local planning policies, settlement boundaries, protected spaces, and infrastructure priorities to help shape future development in the parish alongside Huntingdonshire District Council's Local Plan.

governance.title: Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan Referendum Version Published
governance.summary: Ramsey Town Council advanced the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (2026-2046) to the referendum stage, setting out local policies on built-up area boundaries, protected settlement breaks, community facilities, local green spaces, and sustainable transport.

Cllr M Clarke asked for a recorded vote, Proposed by Cllr M Clarke and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for a recorded vote to be taken. There was insufficient information for Ramsey Town Council to be able to support the application voting FOR Cllrs L Knight, M Clarke and J Clarke. AGAINST Cllrs V Fendley, S Corney E Welsh, J Bufton, S Fice, I Axelsen, A Costello, J Thompson and L Webster. This motion was defeated. The original motion was then discussed ‘To Accept the Planning Application’ Further discussion took place and Cllr S Fice proposed an amendment to the motion ‘To accept the Planning Application with the caveat that

the Highways concerns are addressed.’ This was seconded by Cllr L Webster. Ramsey Town Council voted 9 FOR and 3 ABSTENTIONS for this motion to become the substantive motion. The vote on the substantive motion was then taken ‘To accept the Planning Application with the caveat that the Highways concerns are addressed.’ Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr L Webster Ramsey Town Council voted 9 FOR and 3 ABSTENTIONS to accept the Planning Application with the caveat that the Highways concerns were addressed 340. Planning – other business a) Feedback about the online Planning Training hosted by Huntingdonshire District Council. Members felt it was very monotone and difficult for new members to follow. The training given on new members councillor training was much more informative. b) Feedback on the Development Management Committee reference the David Wilson Homes. Cllr S Corney feedback on the meeting where the Members at the Development Committee (DMC) voted to Refuse the 199 houses Land South of the Maltings, Ramsey. The hearing of the application took over 3.5 hours and between Ramsey Town Council, Bury PC and Sarah Harrington (representing residents) gave comprehensive reasons why the application should be refused. Whilst this was a success, the application will now be taken to the Secretary of State. Cllr S Corney then proposed that Ramsey Town Council seek planning advice about the David Wilson applications that were being developed and heard in smaller phases to stop the developer paying a larger sum for the Community Infrastructure Levy. The amount was thought to be approx. £6 million pounds the community had missed out on. At the DMC meeting which was recorded, the Agent for David Wilson Homes said he had been working with Huntingdonshire District Council for over two and a half years on the application. Cllr S Corney proposed to seek advice on this point. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr J Clarke Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for Ramsey Town Council to seek planning advice on the cumulative effect on the David Wilson applications. c) To agree the representations to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council in response to their Local Plan consultation (previously circulated) Cllr V Fendley reminded the members the points in the document. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to accept the document to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council in response to their Local Plan. 341. Meeting Dates The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 12th November at 7pm.

MINUTES OF RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL MEETING 
held at 7pm on Thursday 10 September 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:  Councillors: A Austin, I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, S Corney, A 
Costello, V Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, L Knight, R Terrill, J Thompson, and L Webster. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk  
 
297. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Aubin, C Maskell, P Rose and E Welsh. 
 
298.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made. 
 
299. Public Participation. 
There was one member of the public who wished to speak and encouraged the Town Council 
to continue to use Future Scooters for young person training for the skate park. 
 
300. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Councillors voted unanimously to accept the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 
27
th
 August 2026 as a correct record. 
 
301. District Councillor & County Councillor Updates: 
Cllrs H Tobias, and R Coogan attended the meeting, and no apologies were received from 
Cllr K Maheshwari. Cllr Tobias informed the members that he would be looking at the roads 
in the area with the Senior Officer for Highways and would be attending his first County 
Council meeting on 13
th
 October. 
Cllr Coogan informed members that the Local Government Reorganisation has been 
paused. Cllr Coogan informed members that he abstained from the Local Plan knowing it 
would be approved, his party wouldn’t allow them to vote for it but he knew our Council 
wanted it to go through. With the Local Plan going through it would mean the area should get 
more infrastructure. Cllr A Austin asked Cllr Coogan to investigate why the Town Council’s 
application for strategic CIL could not be applied for, for play parks. Cllr S Corney asked Cllr 
Coogan to investigate why there was a hold on the decision on the land at Mews Close due 
to the parking strategy, as it currently is waste land not a car park. 
 Council noted that there had been no mention of provision in the Local Plan for Traveller 
and Gypsy sites.  
 
302. Planning Applications for Consideration. 
1.1 26/01440/FUL Change of use to a SEN day school (Class F1), erection of a rear single 
storey extension, external alterations to existing two-storey rear extension and associated 
works including additional car parking, new landscaping and recreation areas – Westward 
House, Bury Road, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr S Fice Ramsey 
Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to APPROVE the application. 
There were no neighbouring objections. Members did note the County Council concerns on 
the size of the in and out areas, but members felt this could easily be mitigated. 
 
1.2 26/01089/HHFUL Proposed replacement roof to form first floor accommodation, 
demolition of the existing porch and erection of a new single storey porch, erection of a new 
balcony, installation of external insulation and cladding to the existing dwelling and 
associated internal alterations – Living Accommodation Stokes Garage, Ramsey Road, 
Ramsey Forty Foot. Proposed by Cllr A Costello and seconded by Cllr M Clarke, Ramsey 

2 
 
Town council voted UNANNIMOUSLY for the District Council to APPROVE the application. 
There were no neighbouring objections. 
 
  
 
303. Planning – other business 
a) Local Plan 2046 – Cllr V Fendley informed members that Huntingdonshire 
District Council’s Local Plan had been approved and it goes to final consultation 
from 16
th
 September 2026 and ends 28
th
 October 2026. As previously been 
mentioned having a local plan shows an intent to develop and supports getting 
infrastructure. Previously Ramsey Town Council had voted to use the Planning 
Consultant to support the response from Ramsey Town Council. There would be 
comment about the lack of provision for Traveller/Gypsy sites and would also 
include what would be in the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan for the 
site at Stoneman Way proposed by David Wilson Homes.  
b) Neighbourhood Plan Independent Inspector Report Update. Cllr V Fendley 
informed members that the Independent Assessor had read the plan and 
supported the view of no further coalition with Bury Parish. It is proposed that the 
community referendum would take place in December. 
  
304. FINANCE ITEMS 
a) Financial Summary - Cash book to 31/8/26 - Noted 
b) Expenditure Transactions to be approved– Proposed by Cllr L Knight and 
seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to 
APPROVE the expenditure transactions. 
c) To approve the implementation of the Local Government, Pay Award - Pay 
rates and allowances have been increased by 3.3% with effect from 1
st
 April 
2026. Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr L Knight Ramsey Town 
Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to APPROVE the pay award. 
d) Updated Grant Form – Cllr A Austin presented the new guidance on the grant 
forms and the scoring system. Cllr A Austin explained the three tiers which 
would cover the small, medium, and large grant applications. Proposed by Cllr 
A Austin and seconded by Cllr L Webster, Ramsey Town Council voted 
UNANIMOUSLY to APPROVE the grant application form and matrix. 
 
305. Future Scooter Permission 
Future Scooters had asked Ramsey Town Council if they could hold one to one 
training sessions on the QEII Skate Park. Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by 
Cllr L Webster Rasmey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to APPROVE Future 
Scooters holding one-to one sessions at the Skate Park but the skate park would still 
be in use for other residents. 
 
306. Working Party Updates: 
Members had received an update from the Chair of each Working Party- noted 
 
307. Communications Working Party Recommendation: 
a) Draft newsletter – Cllr A Austin explained that the draft would be circulated once 
finalised. 
 
308. Town Mayor’s and Clerk’s Correspondence: 
a) Just Giving Fire Fighter Fund Update – Cllr V Fendley informed members 
that the final amount from the Just giving after they had taken their percentage 
was £4546.55- once all payments had been made there was a surplus of 
£1973.69  

3 
 
At this point Cllr Coogan HDC District Councillor indicated he wished to speak. 
Cllr V Fendley suspended standing orders proposed by S Corney and 
seconded by Cllr J Bufton and Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to 
suspend standing orders to allow Cllr Coogan to speak. Cllr Coogan informed 
members that he would be meeting with National Emergency Fund to support 
residents and businesses. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr J 
Bufton to bring back standing orders, Ramsey Town Council voted 
UNANIMOUSLY to put the Standing Orders back in place. 
Cllr S Corney proposed that the remaining funds were donated to the fire 
fighters Charity as described on the Just giving, Cllr A Austin put in a counter 
proposal to go back to Just Giving and ask the doners to decide on where it 
should go. This was seconded by Cllr M Clarke. Ramsey Town Council voted 
7 FOR 6 AGAINST 1 ABSTENTION, this then became the substantive motion 
proposed by Cllr A Austin and seconded by Cllr M Clarke Ramsey Town 
Council voted 8 FOR, 2 AGAINST and 3 ABSTENTIONS for the Just giving 
doners to be asked who they want the remaining funds to be donated to. 
b) FOI Response on CIL Funding Update- Cllr V Fendley informed members 
that the Freedom of Information request by Cllr K Maheshwari had been 
responded to, within two hours of the response being sent then Cllr K 
Maheshwari had put a post on Facebook with all the information given. A 
further Freedom of Information request then came in from Cllr K Maheshwari 
who asked for more information on the council’s decision making. Council 
noted the request. 
c) Emergency Planning Meeting – 1
st
 October 6:30pm at Ramsey Community 
Centre. Cllr V Fendley reminded members of the Emergency Planning 
Meeting. 
d) Climate Emergency Briefing- 23
rd
 September at St Thomas a Becket Church 
6pm. Cllr V Fendley informed members of the Climate Emergency Briefing. 
e) Council to decide on centralised headstones in the lawn cemetery- After 
a discussion the Clerk was asked to take the matter back to the Cemetery 
Working Party. 
 
309.Attendances at Meetings and Organisations: 
a) Cllr V Fendley and Cllr S Corney attended the1940 Drumhead Service 
b) Heritage Day – Councillor Support. Cllr V Fendley thanked the Councillors for 
the support they would be giving at the Mortuary Chapel on Heritage Day. 
 
      310. District Wide Dog PSPO Renewal – Consultation- proposed by Cllr S 
Corney and seconded by Cllr R Terrill, Ramsey town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY 
to APPROVE the renewal of the District Wide Dog PSPO. 
 
311. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 24th September 
at 7pm.

held at 7pm on Thursday 24 September 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:    Councillors: A Austin, I Axelsen, J Clarke, M Clarke, V Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, 
L Knight, P Rose, R Terrill, J Thompson, and L Webster. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk  
 
312. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Bufton, S Corney (representing the Council at RAF Wyton) A Costello, C Maskell, and 
E Welsh. 
 
313.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made. 
 
314. Public Participation. 
There was one member of the public who wished to thank the Town Council for awarding her 
the Freedom of the Town. 
 
315. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Proposed by Cllr A Austin and seconded by Cllr R Terrill, Councillors voted unanimously to 
accept the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 10
th
 September 2026 as a correct 
record. 
 
316. Planning Applications for Consideration. 
1.1 25/01382/OUT Outline application with all matters reserved save for access for erection 
of up to 199 dwellings including open space, play space, car parking, drainage, utilities 
connections and the construction of a new access off Stoneman Way and Biggin Lane – 
further information received. Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr P Rose Ramsey 
Town Council members voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to REFUSE the 
application. The traffic assessment had not been actioned on the correct miles per hour- it 
stated 30mph when it is 20mph road. It is in Bury Parish Council’s adopted Local Plan and in 
the Draft Local Plan for Ramsey that the land needs to remain undeveloped to stop further 
coalescence between Bury Village and Ramsey Town. Drainage remains a concern for 
members for the area of land not having enough drainage in place and water would then be 
flowing into Slade Dyke. 
 
1.2 26/00681/FUL Construction of 2 drive-thru units (sui generis) with associated hard and 
soft landscaping – Plot 09A St Marys Road, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr P Rose and seconded 
by Cllr S Fice Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to 
APPROVE the application.  
 
1.3 26/01584/FUL Open storage of vehicles (Use Class B8) in association with the adjacent 
vehicle scrapping, recycling, and export businesses – Land South of The Foundry, Factory 
Bank, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr R Terrill Ramsey Town 
Council voted 11 FOR and 1 ABSTENTION for the Clerk to gain further information before a 
formal vote would be submitted. The questions to be asked were, has the land had change of 
use from agricultural land? Has the environmental work been looked at for contamination? 
Has the drainage been looked at? Concerns on the land encroaching the area that would be 
siting the MUGA on the Northern Gateway. 
 
 

2 
 
1.4 26/01670/S73 Variation of condition 2 (Approved Plans – Planning Applications) of 
25/02222/FUL – Land Rear of 192 Oilmills Road, Ramsey Mereside. Proposed by Cllr S 
Fice and seconded by Cllr M Clarke Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the 
District Council to APPROVE the application. Council saw no reason to object to the 
variations being made 
317. Planning – other business 
a) Somersham Neighbourhood Plan Consultation Ramsey Town Council comments 
to be agreed. Ramsey Town Council comments were to wish them well with their 
Local Plan. 
b) Street Naming: Equestrian Facilities, Land on south side of Middle Drove, Ramsey 
Heights to be known as The Meadows, Middle Drove, Ramsey Heights. Noted 
 
c) Huntingdonshire Pre Submission Local Plan – 2046, Ramsey Town Council 
response – Email received regarding Site Allocation Bury 1 (Old Station Road, Bury 
development) – previously circulated. Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr A 
Austin the members voted UNANIMOUSLY for the Clerk to forward the email to the 
Planning consultant to add into their response. 
 
d) Mews Car Park and Great Whyte Improvements Update – The Mayor Cllr V 
Fendley updated the members on the two meetings she had had with the Portfolio 
holder for Governance about the Pedestrianisation Project. They felt it was a positive 
project and could see the benefits it would bring to the town. The Portfolio Holder also 
felt the land at the back of the Doctors on Mews Close was required for parking and 
asked the District Council team to move forward with the agreement of a Town 
Council lease hold of 50 years. He encouraged the Mayor to apply for this round of 
the HDC CIL funding to enable the work. 
 
318. Residents Communication. 
a) Draft newsletter – Cllr A Austin tabled the newsletter which was authorised to go to 
print. 
 
319. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 8th October at 
7pm.
